Europe · Europa
In plain words · In gewone woorden

Why the freezer attacks are also a story about our electricity. The same kind of small computer that was used to heat the freezers also switches solar parks, batteries and charging points. This page says what is proven, what is not, what is missing in the law and what to ask for. It then goes through every kind of energy one by one: nuclear, gas, oil, wind at sea, dams, heating and charging points.

NL: Waarom de diepvriesaanvallen ook over onze elektriciteit gaan. Hetzelfde soort kleine computer waarmee de diepvriezers opgewarmd werden, schakelt ook zonneparken, batterijen en laadpalen. Deze pagina zegt wat bewezen is, wat niet, wat er in de wet ontbreekt en wat hij kan vragen. Daarna komt elke energiebron apart aan bod: kernenergie, gas, olie, wind op zee, stuwdammen, warmtenetten en laadpalen.

Energy and the grid: the national-security angle

Why the freezer attacks and the attacks on power systems are one story, what is proven and what is not, where the law falls short, what could be asked for, and every energy source one by one: grid, solar and wind, nuclear, gas, oil, sea cables, dams, heating and charging points.

The point in one sentence. The freezers were hit through a small computer that switches a heavy electrical machine and that could be reached over the internet; the same kind of computer, with the same weakness, switches our solar parks, batteries, heat pumps and charging points, and in Poland attackers already went for the power system itself.
NL: De diepvriezers werden getroffen via een kleine computer die een zware elektrische machine schakelt en die via het internet bereikbaar was; hetzelfde soort computer, met dezelfde zwakte, schakelt onze zonneparken, batterijen, warmtepompen en laadpalen, en in Polen gingen aanvallers al voor het stroomsysteem zelf.

How a freezer attack is also an energy story

In plain words

A supermarket freezer is a big electrical machine with a small computer on it. Someone at a distance told that computer to heat instead of cool. Now replace "freezer" with "solar park", "home battery", "heat pump" or "charging point". They work the same way: a machine that takes power from the grid or puts power into it, with a small computer that an installer or a manufacturer controls over the internet. One such machine doesn't matter. But the grid only stays up when the power going in equals the power going out, every second. If someone switches thousands of these machines off or on at the same moment, that balance breaks, and a whole region can go dark.

NL: Een supermarktdiepvriezer is een grote elektrische machine met een kleine computer erop. Iemand zei van op afstand tegen die computer dat hij moest verwarmen in plaats van koelen. Vervang nu "diepvriezer" door "zonnepark", "thuisbatterij", "warmtepomp" of "laadpaal". Ze werken op dezelfde manier: een machine die stroom van het net haalt of erop zet, met een kleine computer die een installateur of een fabrikant via het internet bedient. Eén zo'n machine maakt niets uit. Maar het net blijft alleen overeind als er elke seconde evenveel stroom in gaat als eruit. Wie duizenden van die machines op hetzelfde ogenblik uit- of aanschakelt, breekt dat evenwicht, en dan kan een hele regio zonder stroom vallen.

  • The freezers are themselves part of the energy system. The maker of the attacked controllers sells them as a way to help balance the grid: its own technical paper estimates that 500 supermarkets together can shift about 26 megawatts. In France about 700 sites were hit in one night. That is small next to a national grid; the point is that the method works on electrical machines at scale.
  • The same weakness has been found in energy equipment. In October 2026 Dutch researchers (Modat with the Dutch national cyber centre) found 8,547 control systems at European wind and solar parks that could be reached from the internet and should not be: 7,942 at solar parks and 605 at wind farms, in 35 countries. No Belgian figure was published.
  • The risk is the platform behind the devices. The Dutch inspectorate for digital infrastructure warned in October 2026 that a break-in or a faulty update at one manufacturer's or installer's online platform could switch enough inverters, home batteries, heat pumps and chargers at once to destabilise the grid.
  • The actors overlap. France attributes its freezer wave to a unit of Iran's Revolutionary Guards. In November 2023 the United States linked a Revolutionary Guards group to the takeover of controllers at American water utilities. Russia's FSB is held responsible for the Polish energy attack.
What is proven and what is not. Proven: the device type, the method and the actors overlap, and energy systems are being targeted. Not proven, and not to be said: that the freezer attacks touched the electricity grid, or that the Belgian grid has been hacked. No public source reports a successful attack on Elia or Fluvius. The Belgian freezer wave has not been attributed to anyone.

The evidence, in date order

  1. Dec 2015
    Ukraine: the first blackout by hackersConfirmed

    Attackers switched off substations from a distance; about 225,000 customers lost power for hours. A second attack hit Kyiv in December 2016.

  2. May 2023
    Denmark: 22 energy companies in a few daysConfirmed

    The largest attack on Danish critical infrastructure. Most break-ins worked because firewalls had not been updated (SektorCERT). Who did it is disputed.

  3. Nov 2023
    United States: water controllers taken overConfirmed

    A group the US links to Iran's Revolutionary Guards took over industrial controllers at water utilities. Same kind of device, same kind of open door.

  4. Nov 2024
    Lithuania closes the remote doorConfirmed

    A law limits the ability of Chinese manufacturers to reach Lithuanian solar and wind plants from a distance.

  5. 28 Apr 2025
    Spain and Portugal: a blackout that was not an attackConfirmed

    A technical failure, not hackers (final expert report, March 2026). It showed what a day without power does to a modern country.

  6. 29 Dec 2025
    Poland: attack on about 30 energy sitesConfirmed

    Heat-and-power plants and the systems that manage wind and solar. It failed; it could have left 500,000 people without power in winter. In July 2026 the EU and the UK held Russia's FSB responsible and imposed sanctions.

  7. Feb 2026
    Fluvius tells its investorsConfirmed

    In an official document for investors, Fluvius writes that its grid is vulnerable to sabotage, terrorism and cyberattacks, and that it has seen a significant increase in cybercrime since 2022. A standard risk warning, not an incident.

  8. May 2026
    EU stops paying for high-risk invertersConfirmed

    The Commission blocks EU funding for energy projects that use inverters from suppliers it considers high-risk, such as Huawei, with a deadline of 1 November 2026. It is a funding rule, not a rule for the market. An EU Commissioner is reported as saying that 80% of the inverters the EU imports are Chinese.

  9. 2026
    Belgium rehearsesConfirmed

    In the European exercise Cyber Europe 2026, energy was among the sectors hit hardest in the Belgian scenario, with transport, public administration and health care (CCB). An exercise, not an attack.

  10. 6–17 Oct 2026
    Three warnings in two weeksConfirmed

    8,547 exposed control systems at wind and solar parks (6 Oct). European grid security experts in Brussels: some household energy devices accept commands without checking who sends them, and weaknesses in such devices have already been exploited (8 Oct). The Dutch inspectorate: the rules should look at how much power a company can switch from a distance, not at how big the company is (17 Oct).

  11. 11 Oct – 2 Nov 2026
    The freezersConfirmed

    France, then Belgium and other countries. In early November five US agencies warned that the same attacks can cause fires and losses in America too.

Why this is national security, in plain words

In plain words

Everything else runs on electricity. Without power there is no water pressure after a few hours, no payment terminal, no mobile network once the batteries of the masts are empty, no trains, no traffic lights, and hospitals run on generators with a limited supply of fuel. An attacker who can switch off power does not need to attack the hospital, the bank and the railway one by one. That is why energy is at the top of the list of vital sectors in European law, and why a weak password on an energy device is not an IT detail but a question of national security.

NL: Al de rest draait op elektriciteit. Zonder stroom is er na enkele uren geen waterdruk meer, geen betaalterminal, geen gsm-netwerk zodra de batterijen van de masten leeg zijn, geen treinen, geen verkeerslichten, en ziekenhuizen draaien op generatoren met een beperkte voorraad brandstof. Een aanvaller die de stroom kan uitschakelen, hoeft het ziekenhuis, de bank en het spoor niet één voor één aan te vallen. Daarom staat energie bovenaan de lijst van vitale sectoren in de Europese wet, en daarom is een zwak wachtwoord op een energietoestel geen IT-detail maar een kwestie van nationale veiligheid.

Who holds what in Belgium: Elia runs the high-voltage grid. Fluvius (Flanders), ORES and RESA (Wallonia) and Sibelga (Brussels) run the local grids. The CREG is the federal energy regulator. The FANC supervises nuclear sites. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium coordinates cyber incidents. The federal energy minister and the regional energy ministers share the policy. In Parliament, the energy laws and the cyber laws go through the same committee, ITRE.

Where the law falls short on energy

aThe rules look at the size of the company, not at the power it can switch

The European cyber law for vital organisations (NIS2) applies from a certain company size. A small installer or app company that can switch thousands of home installations from one screen can fall outside it. For you: the firm that can switch your neighbourhood's solar panels may have fewer duties than your local bakery chain.

bSafe devices become compulsory only in December 2027

The European law for safe products (Cyber Resilience Act) applies to products sold from 11 December 2027, and for these devices the maker checks itself. Everything installed before then stays as it is, for the fifteen to twenty years it sits on a roof.

cThe grid rulebook stops at the big players

Europe has a specific cyber rulebook for electricity (the network code on cybersecurity, in force since 2024). It covers the organisations that matter for power flows between countries. It does not reach the inverter on a roof or the installer's laptop. Its first Europe-wide risk assessment is only starting in 2026.

dOne login for thousands of installations

Installers and manufacturers manage whole fleets from one online platform. Whoever steals that one login has them all. There is no specific duty to protect that login with a second lock.

eNobody has the full picture in Belgium

An inverter needs a technical approval before it may be connected (through Synergrid, the federation of grid operators). That approval is about electrical behaviour, not about who can reach the device over the internet. No public figure was found for how many Belgian energy systems are exposed.

fThe funding rule is not a market rule

Since 1 November 2026 Europe no longer pays for high-risk inverters in projects it funds. Anyone can still buy and connect them with their own money. A rule for the whole market is only possible under the new cyber law now in Parliament.

What to ask for

  1. Duties by megawatts, not by headcount. Whoever can switch more than a set amount of power from a distance gets the duties of a vital organisation, however small the firm. Plain words: if you can switch a neighbourhood, you are treated like a power plant. Route: NIS2 review and the Cybersecurity Act 2.
  2. An independent test for everything connected to the grid. Inverters, batteries, heat pumps and charging points are tested by an independent body before sale, instead of the maker approving itself. Route: the Cyber Resilience Act's list of critical products; European certification under the Cybersecurity Act 2.
  3. No remote switch that Europe cannot control. Remote control only through channels that check who is sending the command and keep a record, hosted under European law; none at all for suppliers classed as high-risk. Route: Cybersecurity Act 2, high-risk supplier rules. This is idea 24 in the list of 53.
  4. A second lock on every platform that manages a fleet. Compulsory for installers, manufacturers and energy apps. Costs almost nothing.
  5. Find the open doors before the attacker does. The national cyber centre scans for exposed energy systems, warns the owner and the installer, and the door must be closed within a fixed number of days. The same rule proposed after the freezers.
  6. Devices must keep working safely on their own. If the connection to the manufacturer is cut, the installation keeps running in a safe setting. Then closing a dangerous remote door doesn't switch off anyone's solar panels.
  7. A Belgian and a European stress test. Grid operators and the cyber centre test once a year what happens if many small devices are switched at once, and publish the main conclusions.

Numbers for this subject

  • 8,547 control systems at European wind and solar parks reachable from the internet, in 35 countries (Modat and the Dutch cyber centre, October 2026).
  • About 30 Polish energy sites attacked on one day; 500,000 people could have lost power.
  • 22 Danish energy companies broken into within a few days in 2023.
  • About 225,000 Ukrainian customers without power after the 2015 attack.
  • About 700 French supermarket sites sabotaged in one night through their refrigeration controllers.
  • 11 December 2027: the date from which new connected devices must be secure by law.

Every energy source, one by one

For each kind of energy: what can go wrong, what has actually happened, how it stands in Belgium, and what to be careful about. Where nothing is on record, it says so.

aNuclear · Kernenergie

What can go wrong, in plain words: A reactor's safety systems are kept apart from the internet by design, and a plant can be shut down by hand. What attackers can reach are the things around it: office networks, suppliers, staff, and the airspace above. So the realistic risks are spying, stolen plans, a forced precautionary shutdown, and fear.

NL: De veiligheidssystemen van een reactor worden bewust gescheiden gehouden van het internet, en een centrale kan met de hand worden stilgelegd. Wat aanvallers wel kunnen bereiken, is alles eromheen: kantoornetwerken, leveranciers, personeel en het luchtruim erboven. De realistische risico's zijn dus spionage, gestolen plannen, een gedwongen voorzorgsstop, en angst.

What is on record:

  • 2010, Iran: the Stuxnet program destroyed uranium centrifuges that were not connected to the internet; it came in on USB sticks. The proof that "not connected" is not the same as "safe".
  • 2014, South Korea: the nuclear operator KHNP was hacked and plans were published. 2016, Germany: malware was found on a computer at the Gundremmingen plant, without effect on operation. 2019, India: malware in the office network of the Kudankulam plant.
  • Oct 2024, United Kingdom: the nuclear site Sellafield was fined £332,500 for four years of cybersecurity failings (2019–2023). The regulator found no sign that the weaknesses had been used.
  • 9 Nov 2025, Belgium: five drones flew over the Doel plant for about an hour (Engie). No effect on operation.
  • Mar 2026, Poland: the National Centre for Nuclear Research said it blocked an attack on its computer systems; the research reactor kept running. First signs pointed to Iran; not confirmed.
  • Nov 2026: Russia and Ukraine accused each other of hacking emergency-alert apps that sent false radiation warnings. No plant was touched: the target was public fear.

In Belgium: Two reactors run: Doel 4 and Tihange 3, restarted in 2025 after the phase-out law was repealed. The Federal Agency for Nuclear Control (FANC) supervises safety and security, with its own rules for nuclear sites. Operator: Engie Electrabel.

Careful: Never "100% safe", never any detail of protection measures, and never suggest a hacker can cause a meltdown from a laptop.

bGas and LNG · Gas en lng

What can go wrong, in plain words: Gas travels through pipelines whose valves and compressors are run by control computers, and arrives by ship at terminals. An attacker can stop the flow by hitting those computers, or simply by hitting the office systems so the operator shuts down as a precaution. Pipelines on the seabed can also be cut physically.

NL: Gas stroomt door pijpleidingen waarvan de kleppen en compressoren door stuurcomputers bediend worden, en komt per schip aan in terminals. Een aanvaller kan de stroom stoppen door die computers te treffen, of gewoon door de kantoorsystemen te treffen, zodat de beheerder uit voorzorg alles stillegt. Pijpleidingen op de zeebodem kunnen ook fysiek doorgesneden worden.

What is on record:

  • May 2021, United States: the Colonial fuel pipeline shut for about six days after ransomware in its office systems; the attackers got in with one stolen password that had no second lock. Petrol stations ran dry.
  • Sep 2022: the Nord Stream gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea were blown up. Oct 2023: the Balticconnector gas pipeline between Finland and Estonia was damaged by a ship's anchor.
  • 29 Jan 2026, Slovenia: probable ransomware at gas supplier Geoplin, with limited effect (CERT-EU).
  • Jul 2026, United Kingdom: an incident disrupted a small gas-fired generator for several days, without customers losing power.
  • No cyberattack on Fluxys or the Zeebrugge terminal was found in public sources.

In Belgium: Belgium is a gas crossroads for north-west Europe: the Zeebrugge LNG terminal and the pipelines to the UK, the Netherlands, Germany and France. Fluxys runs the network; the CREG regulates it. Gas is on the list of vital sectors in the European cyber law.

Careful: Don't say Fluxys or Zeebrugge has been hacked. Nothing public supports it.

cOil, fuel and the port · Olie, brandstof en de haven

What can go wrong, in plain words: Fuel is stored in tank terminals where loading and unloading is run by software. When that software stops, ships and trucks cannot be loaded, even though the fuel is there.

NL: Brandstof wordt opgeslagen in tankterminals waar het laden en lossen door software gestuurd wordt. Als die software stilvalt, kunnen schepen en vrachtwagens niet geladen worden, ook al is de brandstof er.

What is on record:

  • Jan–Feb 2022, Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany: ransomware hit oil terminals in the same days: SEA-Tank in Antwerp, Evos in Ghent and Terneuzen, and Oiltanking in Germany. Loading and unloading were disrupted; Belgian prosecutors opened an investigation.
  • Aug 2026, United States: hackers broke into the propulsion system of an oil tanker before it reached Texas (FBI and US Coast Guard).
  • 11 Nov 2026: a data company was reported to have tried to fly drones with heat cameras over fuel tanks in Rotterdam, Amsterdam and Antwerp, apparently to measure stocks. Spying, not sabotage.
  • No cyberattack on a European refinery or fuel depot in 2025–2026 was found.

In Belgium: The Port of Antwerp-Bruges holds one of Europe's largest clusters of refineries and chemical plants. Drug gangs already try to get into port computer systems (idea 50). Oil is a vital sector in the European cyber law.

Careful: The 2022 attack was by criminals for ransom; don't present it as a state attack.

dOffshore wind and sea cables · Wind op zee en zeekabels

What can go wrong, in plain words: Wind farms at sea are run from land over data links, and their power comes ashore through a few cables. Cut the data link and nobody can control the turbines; cut the power cable and the electricity doesn't arrive.

NL: Windparken op zee worden van op het land bediend via dataverbindingen, en hun stroom komt aan land via een paar kabels. Valt de dataverbinding weg, dan kan niemand de turbines bedienen; wordt de stroomkabel doorgesneden, dan komt de elektriciteit niet aan.

What is on record:

  • 24 Feb 2022, Germany: on the day Russia invaded Ukraine, an attack on a satellite network cut the remote control of about 5,800 Enercon wind turbines. They kept turning, but could not be managed from a distance for weeks. Attributed to Russia.
  • Mar–Apr 2022: turbine maker Nordex and maintenance firm Deutsche Windtechnik were both hit by ransomware.
  • 29 Dec 2025, Poland: the systems that manage wind and solar farms were among the roughly 30 energy sites attacked.
  • Since early 2024 at least 11 data and power cables on the seabed were damaged, mostly in the Baltic Sea. 31 Dec 2025: a cable in the Gulf of Finland; a cargo ship was seized.
  • Oct 2026: 605 control systems at European wind farms were found reachable from the internet (Modat and the Dutch cyber centre).
  • 2026: ships lingering and drones near North Sea wind farms were reported to the British security services. No sabotage in the Belgian North Sea is on record.

In Belgium: Belgium has about 2.3 gigawatts of wind power in its part of the North Sea and is building an energy island there. Elia runs the connection to shore; the navy and the Maritime Security Centre watch the sea.

Careful: Don't say Belgian wind farms or cables have been sabotaged.

eDams and hydropower · Stuwdammen en waterkracht

What can go wrong, in plain words: Gates and valves of dams are opened and closed by control panels, some of them reachable over the internet. Whoever gets in can release water.

NL: De sluizen en kleppen van stuwdammen worden geopend en gesloten via bedieningspanelen, waarvan sommige via het internet bereikbaar zijn. Wie binnenraakt, kan water laten wegstromen.

What is on record:

  • 7 Apr 2025, Norway: hackers opened a valve of a dam at Bremanger and let 500 litres of water per second flow for about four hours before anyone noticed. No damage. In August 2025 Norway's security service blamed pro-Russian hackers: the first time Oslo formally pointed at Moscow for a cyberattack. They did it to show that they could.

In Belgium: Belgium has little hydropower; the main site is the pumped-storage plant at Coo, which works as a large battery for the grid.

Careful: It was a small dam and nobody was in danger; don't inflate it.

fDistrict heating · Warmtenetten

What can go wrong, in plain words: In a heat network one plant heats water for hundreds of buildings. Its controllers decide how hot the water is. Fool the controllers and the heating stops.

NL: In een warmtenet verwarmt één installatie water voor honderden gebouwen. De stuurkastjes bepalen hoe warm het water is. Wie die kastjes misleidt, legt de verwarming stil.

What is on record:

  • 22–23 Jan 2024, Ukraine: an attack on the heating company of Lviv cut the heating of more than 600 apartment buildings for about two days, in freezing weather. The attackers had entered nine months earlier through an internet router that was never updated, and the heating controllers were not separated from the rest of the network.
  • 29 Dec 2025, Poland: combined heat-and-power plants were among the targets.

In Belgium: Heat networks are growing in Flemish cities. District heating is named as a vital sector in the European cyber law.

Careful: This happened in a country at war; say so.

gCharging points for electric cars · Laadpalen

What can go wrong, in plain words: A charging point is a heavy electrical switch connected to the internet and managed by a company from a distance. Thousands of them switched on or off together pull on the grid like a power plant.

NL: Een laadpaal is een zware elektrische schakelaar die met het internet verbonden is en door een bedrijf van op afstand beheerd wordt. Duizenden laadpalen die samen aan- of uitgeschakeld worden, trekken aan het net zoals een centrale.

What is on record:

  • Jun–Jul 2026: researchers scanning the internet found that 72% of the charging-point connections they could see sent their data without encryption.
  • Mar 2026: the US cyber agency warned of critical flaws in a widely used management system for charging points: an attacker could pretend to be a charger and take over as administrator.
  • The most used technical standard for charging points dates from 2015 and has no built-in encryption.
  • No attack that destabilised a grid through charging points is on record.

In Belgium: The number of charging points in Belgium grows fast, driven by company cars. Charging points fall under the European safe-product law only for products sold from 11 December 2027.

Careful: A risk shown by researchers, not an attack that has happened.

hCoal and gas power plants, and hydrogen · Kolen- en gascentrales, en waterstof

What can go wrong, in plain words: Large power plants are better protected than small devices, but their office systems are hit like any company's, and a plant may slow down or stop as a precaution.

NL: Grote centrales zijn beter beschermd dan kleine toestellen, maar hun kantoorsystemen worden getroffen zoals bij elk bedrijf, en een centrale kan uit voorzorg vertragen of stilvallen.

What is on record:

  • Dec 2025, Romania: ransomware in the business systems of the Oltenia Energy Complex, which produces about 30% of the country's electricity. The power system stayed stable.
  • Late 2024, Romania: the electricity supplier Electrica was breached by a ransomware group.
  • Hydrogen: no cyber incident at a hydrogen installation was found. It is on the list of vital sectors in the European cyber law, so the same duties apply as the sector grows.

In Belgium: Belgium's gas-fired plants keep the lights on when wind and sun fall short. They fall under the strictest tier of the cyber law.

Careful: The power supply was not interrupted in either Romanian case.

What the evidence does not support

  • Not "the freezer attack was an attack on our grid". It was an attack on the same kind of equipment.
  • Not "the Spanish blackout was a cyberattack". It was not.
  • Not "our grid has been hacked" or "a blackout is coming". No source supports either.
  • Not a number for exposed Belgian energy systems. None has been published.
  • Not "Chinese inverters contain kill switches" as a fact. The verified point is the remote access through the manufacturer's platform.
  • No details about the protection of nuclear sites.

Europe · Europa
In plain words · In gewone woorden

Where attackers reached water plants and dams in the other 30 countries, how they got in, and who was blamed.

NL: Waar aanvallers waterinstallaties en dammen bereikten in de andere 30 landen, hoe ze binnenkwamen, en wie de schuld kreeg.

Water: the other 30 countries

Attacks on drinking water, waste water and dams in the other 26 EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, 2025 and 2026. Something is on record for 7 countries; for 23 nothing was found.

In plain words

In three countries attackers reached the machinery itself: a valve opened at a Norwegian dam, pipes burst at a Danish waterworks, and five Polish treatment plants had their controls taken over. All three got in the same simple way: a weak or factory password on a control panel that could be reached from the internet. In Romania and Spain the offices were hit by ransomware but the water kept flowing, because offices and machinery were kept apart. For most countries nothing is on record.

NL: In drie landen raakten aanvallers tot bij de machines zelf: een klep geopend aan een Noorse dam, gesprongen leidingen bij een Deens waterbedrijf, en vijf Poolse zuiveringsinstallaties waarvan de besturing werd overgenomen. Alle drie kwamen op dezelfde eenvoudige manier binnen: een zwak of standaardwachtwoord op een bedieningspaneel dat vanaf het internet bereikbaar was. In Roemenië en Spanje werden de kantoren getroffen door ransomware, maar het water bleef stromen, omdat kantoren en machines gescheiden waren. Voor de meeste landen is niets bekend.

Labels. Confirmed stated by the organisation, an authority or a court. Reported in the press, not verified. Suspected believed, not proven. Claimed said by one party (a government, a minister) without evidence shown in public or tested in court. Two labels on one line: the first is for the event, the second for who was behind it.

Did they reach the machinery?

CountryWhat was reachedWay inWho, and how firm

Denmark, late 2024Water pressure; three pipes burstWeaker, cheaper securityIntelligence service blames Russia (Dec 2025)

Counts and assessments by others

  • The EU cyber agency ENISA ranks drinking water and waste water among the least mature sectors it assessed (2026). Confirmed
  • The water sector's own information centre (WaterISAC) says water companies were the largest group of targets seen in activist-hacker activity in 2025. Claimed
  • United States, from 27 July 2026: water companies in at least seven states reported attackers changing settings on control devices reachable from the internet (FBI). Outside Europe, kept as the warning case. Confirmed

Countries with something on record

Denmark 2 on record

  • Late 2024: Attackers changed the water pressure at the Tureby Alkestrup waterworks near Køge; at least three pipes burst and homes were left without water. The head of the waterworks said it happened after a switch to cheaper, weaker security. Confirmed
  • 19 Dec 2025: The Danish Defence Intelligence Service publicly blamed Russia: the attack was carried out by the pro-Russian group Z-Pentest, which the service says the Russian state uses as an instrument. Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador. Denmark's first public attribution of this kind. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: A small waterworks saved money on security and pipes burst.NL – Wat het toont: Een klein waterbedrijf bespaarde op beveiliging en de leidingen sprongen.

Germany 2 on record

  • Late Jun 2026: The municipal utilities of Kamen, Bönen and Bergkamen were attacked; the customer portal and direct debits failed, the supply did not. Reported
  • 2026: Only water suppliers serving 500,000 people or more fall under the German rules for critical infrastructure; most are below that line. No case found of attackers taking over the controls of a German water plant. Reported

What it shows: Most German water suppliers are too small to fall under the strict rules.NL – Wat het toont: De meeste Duitse waterbedrijven zijn te klein om onder de strenge regels te vallen.

Netherlands 1 on record

  • 11 Aug 2025: The intelligence service warned that Dutch water and power companies had been targeted; an official said Russia is "embedding itself" in vital sectors so it can disrupt them later. No disruption so far. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: A warning about attackers getting ready, not about damage done.NL – Wat het toont: Een waarschuwing over aanvallers die zich voorbereiden, niet over aangerichte schade.

Norway 2 on record

  • 7 Apr 2025: Attackers opened a valve at a dam in Bremanger and let about 500 litres of water per second run for four hours before it was noticed. No damage. The way in was a weak password on a control panel reachable from the internet. Confirmed
  • Aug 2025: The head of the security service attributed it to pro-Russian hackers. The Russian embassy called that unfounded. One legal study notes that no formal written attribution has been published. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: One weak password moved real water.NL – Wat het toont: Eén zwak wachtwoord zette echt water in beweging.

Poland 3 on record

  • 2025: Attackers got into the control systems of five water treatment plants: Jabłonna Lacka, Szczytno, Małdyty, Tolkmicko and Sierakowo. They had administrator rights and could change pump settings and alarm limits. The way in: factory passwords never changed and control systems reachable from the internet. From the security agency's report of May 2026. Confirmed
  • 2025: Who did it: the agency's report names Russian and Belarusian state groups in general, but did not formally pin these five break-ins on them. Researchers call the attribution unconfirmed. Suspected
  • Aug 2025: The deputy prime minister said an attempt to break into the water supply of a large Polish city had been stopped. The city was not named. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: The clearest European case: five plants, default passwords, open to the internet.NL – Wat het toont: Het duidelijkste Europese geval: vijf installaties, standaardwachtwoorden, open naar het internet.

Romania 1 on record

  • Dec 2025: Ransomware hit the national water authority Apele Române: about 1,000 computer systems affected. Dams and water operations kept running. The attackers used a standard Windows encryption tool. Nobody claimed it and the authority named nobody. Confirmed

What it shows: The offices went down; the dams did not, because the two were separate.NL – Wat het toont: De kantoren vielen uit; de dammen niet, omdat de twee gescheiden waren.

Spain 2 on record

  • 21 Apr 2025: Ransomware at Aigües de Mataró, which serves about 130,000 people: internal systems encrypted, customer data exposed. Supply and water quality not affected (company statement). The year is inferred; the report found gives only the day. Confirmed
  • 3 Jul 2026: The public water company Acosol (Málaga) reported an attack that affected its information systems and may have exposed customer data. Reported

What it shows: Office systems and customer data were hit, not the water.NL – Wat het toont: Kantoorsystemen en klantgegevens werden geraakt, niet het water.

Nothing found

Austria, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Finland, France, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Sweden, Switzerland.

Nothing found means nothing came up in searches in English and the main national languages on 15 November 2026. It is not proof that nothing happened: small water companies rarely make the news, and many countries do not publish incidents.

What it shows: Water is attacked less often than hospitals or town halls, but it is where attackers have most often reached real machinery. The three cases where that happened share one cause that costs almost nothing to fix: a control panel on the open internet with a weak password.NL – Wat het toont: Water wordt minder vaak aangevallen dan ziekenhuizen of gemeentehuizen, maar het is de sector waar aanvallers het vaakst echte machines bereikten. De drie gevallen waar dat gebeurde, hebben één oorzaak gemeen die bijna niets kost om op te lossen: een bedieningspaneel op het open internet met een zwak wachtwoord.

Europe · Europa
In plain words · In gewone woorden

Airports, airlines, ports, ships, rail and freight in the other 30 countries: what was hit, how, and what turned out not to be an attack.

NL: Luchthavens, luchtvaartmaatschappijen, havens, schepen, spoor en vracht in de andere 30 landen: wat geraakt werd, hoe, en wat geen aanval bleek te zijn.

Transport and ports: the other 30 countries

Airports, airlines, ports, shipping, rail and logistics in the other 26 EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, 2025 and 2026. 24 events in 12 countries.

In plain words

Across Europe the pattern is the same as in Belgium: transport is hit through a supplier, and what is lost is mostly data and booking systems, not the planes, ships or trains themselves. One supplier's ransomware slowed airports in four countries. Airlines in France, the Netherlands and Spain lost customer data through outside firms. The rail-pass company Eurail leaked the passports of more than 300,000 travellers. Two cases stand apart: a French ferry where a crew member is charged with planting remote-control software for a foreign state, and the steady disturbance of satellite positioning over the Baltic and now the North Sea. Three big outages that looked like attacks were not: Greece, Italy and the Iberian blackout.

NL: In heel Europa is het patroon hetzelfde als in België: vervoer wordt geraakt via een leverancier, en wat verloren gaat zijn vooral gegevens en boekingssystemen, niet de vliegtuigen, schepen of treinen zelf. De ransomware bij één leverancier vertraagde luchthavens in vier landen. Luchtvaartmaatschappijen in Frankrijk, Nederland en Spanje verloren klantgegevens via externe bedrijven. Het treinpasbedrijf Eurail lekte de paspoorten van meer dan 300.000 reizigers. Twee gevallen staan apart: een Franse veerboot waar een bemanningslid wordt beschuldigd van het plaatsen van afstandsbedieningssoftware voor een buitenlandse staat, en de aanhoudende verstoring van satellietpositionering boven de Oostzee en nu de Noordzee. Drie grote storingen die op aanvallen leken, waren het niet: Griekenland, Italië en de Iberische stroompanne.

Labels. Confirmed stated by the organisation, an authority or a court. Reported in the press, not verified. Suspected believed, not proven. Claimed said by one party (a government, or the attackers themselves) without evidence shown in public. Not proven looked into, nothing found, or denied by the organisation. Two labels on one line: the first is for the event, the second for who was behind it.

By kind of transport

KindWhat happenedWhere

Counts and statements by others

  • The EU cyber agency ENISA says transport has been among the five most attacked sectors for two years; its Europe-wide exercise of 10–11 June 2026, with about 5,000 participants, simulated an attack on rail and shipping. Confirmed
  • Thirteen coastal European countries and Iceland issued a joint statement in January 2026 on growing interference with satellite navigation for shipping in the Baltic and North Sea. Confirmed
  • About 123,000 flights over the Baltic region were affected by signal interference in the first four months of 2025. Quoted by a tracking site without a primary source. Reported
  • A maritime security firm counts 828 cyber incidents in shipping and ports in 2025 against 408 in 2024. A commercial count. Claimed

Countries with something on record

Croatia 1 on record

  • Date not given: The Brodosplit shipyard was hit by the Qilin ransomware group. One mention in a trade report; no date or detail found. Reported

What it shows: One thin report.NL – Wat het toont: Eén mager bericht.

Denmark 2 on record

  • Oct 2025: A new criminal group that targets logistics firms claimed it had stolen data from the freight company DSV. DSV said its operations were not disrupted and its systems were fully working; the claim later vanished from the group's site. Claimed Not proven
  • 11 Nov 2026: The shipping company Maersk confirmed that an attacker reached one older local system, inherited through an earlier takeover, and took data. A ransomware group demands $5 million. Confirmed

What it shows: The world's second-largest container line was reached through a forgotten old system.NL – Wat het toont: De op één na grootste containerrederij ter wereld werd bereikt via een vergeten oud systeem.

France 2 on record

  • Aug 2025: Air France (with KLM) said customer data was taken through an outside supplier, in the week of 28 July. No payment data. Nobody named by the airlines; researchers suspect the criminal group ShinyHunters. Confirmed Suspected
  • Dec 2025: Software that lets an outsider control computers from a distance was found on the passenger ferry GNV Fantastic in the port of Sète. France's domestic intelligence service is investigating; a Latvian crew member was charged with acting for an unnamed foreign power. The ferry company says the attempt was stopped without consequences. Russia was mentioned in the press, not by the authorities; the suspect's lawyer disputes it. Confirmed Suspected

What it shows: A ferry was targeted from the inside, by a crew member, for a foreign state that has not been named.NL – Wat het toont: Een veerboot werd van binnenuit geviseerd, door een bemanningslid, voor een buitenlandse staat die niet genoemd is.

Germany 3 on record

  • 21 May 2025: A joint warning by American, German, Canadian, Australian and other security agencies said that unit 26165 of Russian military intelligence (also known as APT28, a code name) was attacking dozens of logistics and technology firms that move aid to Ukraine, across air, sea and rail. It said the unit had used access to private cameras near border crossings, military sites and railway stations. The warning names sectors, among them ports and airports, not individual ports; a later academic analysis named Hamburg and Rotterdam. Confirmed Claimed
  • 19–20 Sep 2025: Berlin Brandenburg Airport was hit by the same ransomware at the check-in supplier Collins Aerospace as Brussels; average delays of about an hour were reported. Confirmed
  • Feb 2026: Deutsche Bahn's website and booking app were knocked offline by a flood of traffic. Information and booking worked again by 18 February. No customer data stolen. The company would not say who was behind it. Confirmed

What it shows: The trains ran; the booking did not.NL – Wat het toont: De treinen reden; het boeken niet.

Greece 1 on record

  • Jan 2026: A failure of air traffic control radio grounded or disrupted flights for several hours; about 120 flights were grounded at the two largest airports. The government said a cyberattack was unlikely; a judicial inquiry was opened. Confirmed Not proven

What it shows: A big outage that was, as far as known, not an attack.NL – Wat het toont: Een grote storing die, voor zover bekend, geen aanval was.

Ireland 1 on record

  • Sep 2025: Dublin and Cork airports reported smaller effects from the Collins Aerospace ransomware. One source. Reported

What it shows: A side effect of the same supplier attack.NL – Wat het toont: Een neveneffect van dezelfde aanval op een leverancier.

Italy 3 on record

  • Dec 2025: The port authority for the central Adriatic (Ancona) reported an attack, later claimed by the ransomware group Anubis. Whether terminal work was affected is unclear. Confirmed Claimed
  • 7 Feb 2026: Rail sabotage near Bologna and Pesaro on the first full day of the Winter Olympics: a physical attack, described on the page about drones and sabotage. Confirmed
  • Oct 2026: A fault in the national data network forced air traffic control to cut capacity by up to half; full capacity was back the same day. The operator ruled out a cyberattack. Confirmed Not proven

What it shows: The air traffic fault was technical; the rail attack was physical; only the port case was a hack.NL – Wat het toont: De storing in het luchtverkeer was technisch; de aanval op het spoor was fysiek; alleen het havengeval was een hack.

Lithuania 2 on record

  • Since Oct 2025: Vilnius Airport closed more than 20 times because of balloons from Belarus. See the page about drones and sabotage. Confirmed
  • 2026: Lithuania said transmitters in Russia's Kaliningrad region can falsify satellite positioning signals up to 450 km away, covering much of Poland, the Baltic states and part of the Nordic countries. Claimed

What it shows: An airport closed by balloons, under a sky where the positioning signal cannot be trusted.NL – Wat het toont: Een luchthaven gesloten door ballonnen, onder een hemel waar het positiesignaal niet te vertrouwen is.

Netherlands 4 on record

  • Aug 2025: KLM (with Air France) said customer data was taken through an outside supplier. Confirmed
  • 26 Dec 2025: Eurail, the Utrecht company behind the Interrail pass, was breached: data of 308,777 people, including passport details and, for young travellers on the EU's DiscoverEU scheme, bank and health details. In February 2026 the data was offered for sale. Affected people were notified from 27 March 2026. Confirmed
  • Jan 2026: The Amsterdam appeal court gave a hacker seven years for breaking into port systems in Rotterdam and Antwerp in 2020–2021; about 210 kg of cocaine came in through Rotterdam with his help. Confirmed
  • 9 Nov 2026: Dozens of aircraft over the Netherlands and Belgium lost their satellite positioning signal; experts place the source at sea north of Texel and suspect deliberate jamming. Belgium’s own air traffic service later told VRT it had received no reports that day. Update 16 Nov 2026: Dutch air traffic control calls deliberate jamming plausible and says safety was not compromised; seven aircraft had trouble on approach to Schiphol. There is no official finding and nobody is named. Confirmed Suspected

What it shows: Three hundred thousand passports leaked from a rail-pass company, and it took three months to tell the people.NL – Wat het toont: Driehonderdduizend paspoorten gelekt bij een treinpasbedrijf, en het duurde drie maanden om het de mensen te zeggen.

Spain 3 on record

  • Nov 2025: Iberia said customer data was exposed through a supplier; passwords and bank details not affected. The criminal group Everest claims 596 GB and demands $6 million; the airline has not confirmed those figures. Confirmed Claimed
  • 24–25 Mar 2026: Ransomware at the Port of Vigo: digital systems cut off, work continued by hand. A ransom was demanded; group and payment not confirmed. Confirmed
  • 24–26 Sep 2026: The rail companies Adif and Renfe: Adif saw unusual activity on 24 September and its website went down on the 25th; Renfe said customer names and email addresses were reached through Adif's servers, and a later notice mentions identity numbers, journeys and encrypted passwords. Trains ran normally. Press figures of 500 GB and claims that the attack was run by artificial intelligence are not confirmed by either company. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: An airline, a port and the railways in ten months; in each case the service kept running.NL – Wat het toont: Een luchtvaartmaatschappij, een haven en het spoor in tien maanden; telkens bleef de dienst draaien.

Sweden 1 on record

  • 17–18 Sep 2026: Two passenger flights lost satellite navigation over the south-east, near Gotland and Öland; both landed normally on other instruments. One source. The transport agency describes continuous jamming and more organised signal-faking in the region. Reported

What it shows: Signal loss over the Baltic has become routine.NL – Wat het toont: Signaalverlies boven de Oostzee is routine geworden.

Switzerland 1 on record

  • Oct 2025: The same group that named DSV listed the freight company Kuehne+Nagel as a victim. The company said only that it was aware of the mentions. Claimed

What it shows: A claim by criminals, not confirmed.NL – Wat het toont: Een bewering van criminelen, niet bevestigd.

Nothing specific found

Austria, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Finland, Hungary, Iceland, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Malta, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia.

For several of these countries there are physical events that touch transport, described on the page about drones and sabotage: the railway explosion in Poland, the airport closures in Luxembourg, the ships sunk off Romania and Bulgaria, the sea cables off Finland and Estonia, and the false bomb threats at Prague airport. Nothing found means nothing came up in searches on 15 November 2026; it is not proof that nothing happened.

What it shows: Almost nobody attacked a train, a plane or a ship directly. They attacked the companies around them: the check-in supplier, the booking site, the customer database, the freight forwarder. The rule that follows is simple and still rarely applied: know which outside firms you cannot run without, and have a way to work for a week without each of them.NL – Wat het toont: Bijna niemand viel een trein, een vliegtuig of een schip rechtstreeks aan. Ze vielen de bedrijven eromheen aan: de leverancier van de check-in, de boekingssite, de klantendatabank, de expediteur. De regel die daaruit volgt is eenvoudig en wordt nog zelden toegepast: weet zonder welke externe bedrijven je niet kunt draaien, en zorg dat je een week zonder elk van hen kunt werken.

Hospitals and health data in the other 30 countries: where care stopped, where data leaked, and why the supplier is usually the way in.

NL: Ziekenhuizen en gezondheidsgegevens in de andere 30 landen: waar de zorg stilviel, waar gegevens lekten, en waarom de leverancier meestal de weg naar binnen is.

Health: the other 30 countries

Hospitals, clinics, laboratories, health software and patient data in the other 26 EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, 2025 and 2026. 43 entries in 21 countries.

In plain words

Two kinds of damage. The first is care that stops: emergency rooms closed in Germany and Poland, operations postponed, staff back on paper. The second is data that leaks, and here the numbers are far larger and the cause is nearly always the same: not the hospital, but a company that works for hospitals. A French payment operator lost 15.4 million social security numbers; a French software maker's breach may concern more than 15 million people; a Dutch laboratory lost the data of about 941,000 people; a Polish software platform close to 19 million. Almost all of it is crime for money. No state has been blamed for an attack on a hospital in these countries in these two years.

NL: Twee soorten schade. De eerste is zorg die stilvalt: spoedafdelingen gesloten in Duitsland en Polen, operaties uitgesteld, personeel terug op papier. De tweede is gegevens die lekken, en daar zijn de cijfers veel groter en is de oorzaak bijna altijd dezelfde: niet het ziekenhuis, maar een bedrijf dat voor ziekenhuizen werkt. Een Franse betalingsoperator verloor 15,4 miljoen rijksregisternummers; het lek bij een Franse softwaremaker kan meer dan 15 miljoen mensen treffen; een Nederlands laboratorium verloor de gegevens van ongeveer 941.000 mensen; een Pools softwareplatform bijna 19 miljoen. Bijna alles is misdaad voor geld. Voor geen enkele aanval op een ziekenhuis in deze landen is in deze twee jaar een staat aangewezen.

Labels. Confirmed stated by the organisation, an authority or a regulator. Reported in the press, not verified. Claimed said by one party, here mostly criminals on their own sites. Suspected a person arrested or identified, not yet judged. Two labels on one line: the first is for the event, the second for who was behind it.

Counts by others

  • Poland's national e-health centre: 13 ransomware incidents in health care so far in 2026, against 10 in all of 2025. Confirmed
  • France's digital health agency: 15% of care institutions had an incident that disrupted their work between 2022 and 2025. Reported
  • Italy, a sector body: attacks on hospitals up 20% in 2025; 47% were ransomware. Claimed
  • The EU cyber agency: ransomware was 54% of health incidents in 2023 and 45% in 2024; in its 2026 review health is still among the sectors "in the risk zone". An EU support centre for hospitals is to start an early-warning service by 2026 at the latest; whether it has started was not confirmed. Confirmed

  • Date not found: The state IT company said it fought off a very large flood of traffic aimed at the national health information system. Reported

France 8 on record

  • Summer 2025: A private hospital lost the data of 524,867 patients and of 202,246 contact persons. In September 2026 the data regulator fined it €500,000 for inadequate protection of its patient-record system. Confirmed
  • 8 Sep 2025: Public hospitals in the Hauts-de-France region were targeted through the servers that hold patients' identity data. Reported

  • 2 Jul 2026: Chaumont hospital: data lost and critical systems unavailable. Confirmed
  • 20 Sep 2026: Hôpital Paris Saint-Joseph confirmed a leak covering 15,044 patients. Confirmed

The blood service says it was contained quickly, "without impact" on stored products and samples. The Paris prosecutor opened an investigation and gave it to the cybercrime office and the domestic intelligence service. Nobody has been named for this attack.   • Feb 2026: BDH-Klinik Greifswald: the communication network was paralysed and theft of patient data was later confirmed. Confirmed

Reported Claimed

The count of people affected grew from more than 405,000 women to about 941,000 people in later reports. The health inspectorate found it had not met legal security standards. Confirmed
  • 7 Apr 2026: Ransomware at ChipSoft, whose patient-record software runs in 70 to 80% of Dutch hospitals. A criminal group (Embargo) claimed 100 GB; ChipSoft said on 29 April that the stolen data was destroyed. The number of patients was never disclosed. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: One software maker serves most hospitals of a country: when it falls, they all cut the cord.NL – Wat het toont: Eén softwaremaker bedient de meeste ziekenhuizen van een land: als die valt, trekken ze allemaal de stekker uit.

Nothing specific found

Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Malta, Norway, Romania, Slovenia, Sweden.

Most entries on this page were already in the country cards of this file; new here are the French fine, Reims, Greiz, Roth, Portugal, the two Italian cases and the later Dutch count. Nothing found means nothing came up in searches up to 16 November 2026.

What it shows: A hospital can do everything right and still lose its patients' data, because the data also sits with the laboratory, the billing firm, the software maker and the payment operator. The law treats hospitals as vital; many of these suppliers are far smaller and far less checked. The two things that limited the damage were old-fashioned: being able to work on paper for weeks, and keeping the patient files apart from everything else, as Croatia's ministry did.NL – Wat het toont: Een ziekenhuis kan alles goed doen en toch de gegevens van zijn patiënten verliezen, omdat die gegevens ook bij het laboratorium, het facturatiebedrijf, de softwaremaker en de betalingsoperator zitten. De wet behandelt ziekenhuizen als vitaal; veel van deze leveranciers zijn veel kleiner en worden veel minder gecontroleerd. De twee dingen die de schade beperkten, waren ouderwets: wekenlang op papier kunnen werken, en de patiëntendossiers gescheiden houden van al de rest, zoals het Kroatische ministerie deed.

In plain words · In gewone woorden

The same threats in the other 30 countries: what was proven in court, what a government claims, and what fell apart when police looked closely.

NL: Dezelfde dreigingen in de andere 30 landen: wat voor de rechter bewezen is, wat een regering beweert, en wat uiteenviel toen de politie goed keek.

Drones, sabotage and hybrid threats: the other 30 countries

The same subject as the Belgium page, for the other 26 EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, 2025 and 2026. 92 events in 25 countries. Counted apart from the cyber register.

In plain words

Two very different stories sit under the same word. The drone sightings over airports mostly fell apart when police looked closely: Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands and Belgium all ended with no proof. The sabotage is the opposite: it is proven in court. Finland jailed a ship's captain for cutting cables, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania convicted arsonists working for Russian intelligence, Germany formally blamed Russia for a drone with explosives at Leipzig airport, and in October 2026 sailors were killed by drones in EU waters off Romania and Bulgaria.

NL: Onder hetzelfde woord zitten twee heel verschillende verhalen. De dronewaarnemingen boven luchthavens vielen meestal uiteen toen de politie goed keek: Denemarken, Noorwegen, Nederland en België eindigden allemaal zonder bewijs. De sabotage is het omgekeerde: die is bewezen voor de rechter. Finland veroordeelde een kapitein voor het doorsnijden van kabels, Estland, Letland en Litouwen veroordeelden brandstichters die voor de Russische inlichtingendienst werkten, Duitsland gaf Rusland formeel de schuld van een drone met explosieven op de luchthaven van Leipzig, en in oktober 2026 werden zeelieden gedood door drones in EU-wateren voor Roemenië en Bulgarije.

Labels. Confirmed stated by an authority, a court or the organisation itself. Reported in the press, not verified. Suspected believed, not proven. Claimed said by one party (a minister, a government, a think tank) without evidence shown in public or tested in court. Not proven investigated, no evidence found. Two labels on one line: the first is for the event, the second for who or what was behind it. A government blaming Russia is marked Confirmed (it said so) and Claimed (no court has tested it).

  • 151 Russia-linked sabotage incidents in Europe from February 2022 to February 2026, of which 41 newly added: Poland 31, France 20, Lithuania 15, Germany 15, Estonia 11 (ICCT/GLOBSEC, a research count, not an official one). Claimed
  • 144 suspected drone sightings across Europe, 2024–2026 (IISS, a think tank). Claimed

Country by country

Austria 1 on record

  • 20 May 2026: A Vienna court convicted former intelligence officer Egisto Ott of spying for Russia: four years and one month. He passed information to Russian services and to the fugitive Jan Marsalek, including a secure government laptop for €20,000. He has appealed. Confirmed

What it shows: The Austrian problem is spying from the inside, not drones.NL – Wat het toont: Het Oostenrijkse probleem is spionage van binnenuit, niet drones.

Bulgaria 5 on record

  • 10 Aug 2026: Explosion and fire at an ammunition warehouse of the arms maker EMCO, which supplies Ukraine. The interior minister first pointed away from outside causes. Confirmed
  • Aug 2026: A drone exploded near the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline. One source; no official finding. Reported
  • 12 Sep 2026: A second fire at another EMCO depot near Tsareva Livada, 33 days later. Nobody hurt. The minister said sabotage is one of the lines of inquiry and ordered every ammunition depot inspected. Confirmed Suspected
  • Autumn 2026: The state news agency reported that prosecutors see a link between four ammunition-warehouse blasts and suspect Russia. Russia rejects this. Suspected
  • Oct 2026: Drones hit two commercial ships in Bulgaria's economic zone at sea, a first. On 13 October the HS Dignity was struck; 11 sailors missing, five survivors (Bloomberg). The prime minister summoned the Russian ambassador; Bulgaria has not formally blamed Russia. Confirmed Suspected

What it shows: Arms depots that supply Ukraine keep burning, and the war at sea has reached Bulgarian waters.NL – Wat het toont: Wapendepots die Oekraïne bevoorraden blijven branden, en de oorlog op zee heeft de Bulgaarse wateren bereikt.

Croatia 1 on record

  • Aug 2026: One news round-up mentions an arson investigation near Omiš taking a terrorism angle. Not confirmed in a primary source. Reported

What it shows: Nothing solid on record.NL – Wat het toont: Niets hards bekend.

  • Early Mar 2026: Drones hit the British base RAF Akrotiri on the island, damaging a hangar. Cypriot officials said they were launched from Lebanon, probably by Hezbollah, during the Iran war. Not a Russian case. Greece and France sent jets, frigates and anti-drone systems. Confirmed Suspected

What it shows: Cypriot officials say the drones came from Lebanon, probably launched by Hezbollah, not from Russia.NL – Wat het toont: Cypriotische autoriteiten zeggen dat de drones uit Libanon kwamen, waarschijnlijk gelanceerd door Hezbollah, en niet uit Rusland.

Czechia 3 on record

  • 2025: A Prague court sentenced a Colombian man to eight years for an arson attack and for planning another; the case is believed to be possibly linked to Russia. Confirmed Suspected
  • 20 Mar 2026: Arson at a warehouse of the defence firm LPP Holding in Pardubice. Suspects were held in Czechia, Slovakia and later Bulgaria on terrorism charges. A group claimed it over the firm's Israeli ties; Czech intelligence asked publicly whether Russia used that group as cover. Confirmed Suspected
  • Nov 2026: Prague airport was among the worst hit by the Europe-wide hoax bomb threats: nine flights on one day. Reported

What it shows: An arms factory burned, and nobody can yet say for whom.NL – Wat het toont: Een wapenfabriek brandde, en niemand kan al zeggen in wiens opdracht.

Denmark 5 on record

  • 22–23 Sep 2025: Copenhagen Airport closed for about four hours after reports of two or three large drones; at least 35 incoming flights were diverted. Police did not shoot, because of the fuel depots and the full aircraft nearby. On 23 September Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called it "the most serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure to date" and said she could not rule out Russia. Nobody was named. Confirmed Suspected
  • 24 Sep – 2 Oct 2025: 61 reports of drones over Aalborg and military sites in Jutland. Reported
  • 2026: The police district reviewed those 61 reports: no evidence of illegal drone flights that concern security. It withdrew its earlier word "verified". Confirmed Not proven
  • 25 Jun 2026: Police closed the nine-month Copenhagen investigation: no evidence that the flying objects were drones, although drone activity "cannot be ruled out". No suspects. Confirmed Not proven
  • 20 Nov 2026: Denmark's security service PET said Russian intelligence services planned and initiated a plot to kill the Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in Denmark. Two Danish men with links to the banned gang Loyal to Familia are charged and in custody; they were reportedly arrested in September with weapons in their car in Hellerup, shortly before his concert on 25 September, and reportedly plead not guilty. Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said Russia's defence attaché must leave Denmark within seven days. No evidence of the Russian role has been published; the report found does not give a Russian response. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: The case that started Europe's drone alarm ended with no proof of a single drone.NL – Wat het toont: De zaak die het Europese dronealarm startte, eindigde zonder bewijs van één drone.

Estonia 7 on record

  • Jan 2025: Arson at a supermarket in Osula and later at a Ukrainian restaurant in Tallinn. A court sentenced a man to six and a half years and said it was ordered by Russian military intelligence. Date of the verdict not found. Confirmed
  • 31 Dec 2025: The cargo ship Fitburg dragged its anchor about 130 km and damaged cables, partly in Estonia's zone. See Finland for the verdict. Confirmed
  • Aug 2026: Arson at a Tallinn building used by Milrem Robotics, which makes military robots. Three Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia and handed over. Confirmed
  • 29 Sep 2026: The Estonian government and its security service formally said the Milrem arson was "commissioned by Russian security services". The Kremlin denies it. Confirmed Claimed
  • 14 Nov 2026: An attempt to blow up and set fire to the building of the drone maker Threod Systems was stopped at 3:06 at night. Eight Latvian citizens were detained, and prosecutors asked a court to keep five in custody. The security service KAPO said the attack was ordered by Russian military intelligence; it has published no evidence. It is the second attack on an Estonian defence firm in three months. The prime minister asked for the necessary steps to close the border with Russia; see 15 November for the announcement and what is not yet decided. Confirmed Claimed
  • 15 Nov 2026: Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said Estonia would close all road border crossings with Russia from 1 December (the Narva freight rail crossing stays open for now). He says Estonia has clear evidence that Russian military intelligence (GRU) ordered the attempted arson of 14 November at Threod Systems; no evidence has been published. The Foreign Ministry later clarified that the road crossings (Narva, Luhamaa, Koidula) close on 1 December. Interior minister Igor Taro said, per Interfax, that the freight rail crossing at Narva stays open for now. The government has yet to formally decide the scope and duration. Russia denies it: Kremlin spokesman Peskov called the accusation baseless. Suspects have been detained. Reported
  • 21 Nov 2026: The Estonian Defence Forces issued, then lifted, a possible drone-threat alert for Lääne-Viru and Ida-Viru counties through the public EE-ALARM system (alert at 4:42, all clear at 6:49). NATO fighter jets, Turkish Air Force aircraft, were airborne in response. One ERR reader reported hearing a drone at 6:13; no drone is confirmed over Estonia in the report. At the same time the governor of Russia's Leningrad Oblast said air defences had downed drones (the number he gave rose from six to 93), and Finland restricted air and sea traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland. ERR says a similar alert on 11 November came as Ukrainian drones struck the Russian port of Ust-Luga. Confirmed Reported

What it shows: Estonia names Russia quickly and takes cases to court.NL – Wat het toont: Estland wijst Rusland snel aan en brengt zaken voor de rechter.

Finland 4 on record

  • 31 Dec 2025: The Fitburg damaged undersea cables between Finland and Estonia. Confirmed
  • Aug 2026: The appeal court reversed the Eagle S ruling: Finland does have jurisdiction, because the damage was felt there. The case goes back to the lower court; the three accused have left the country. Confirmed
  • 5 Nov 2026: Fitburg: the Russian captain got three and a half years and an Azerbaijani crew member two years and ten months for aggravated sabotage. The court found they acted on purpose. The captain will appeal. The reports found do not say who, if anyone, ordered it. Confirmed

What it shows: The first prison sentences in Europe for cutting sea cables.NL – Wat het toont: De eerste gevangenisstraffen in Europa voor het doorsnijden van zeekabels.

  • 9 Sep 2025: Nine pig heads were left outside mosques around Paris. Three Serbs were later convicted in Serbia (house arrest) for acts in France and Germany; Serbia's interior ministry said the group was trained by a man acting for a foreign intelligence service. No state was named by a court. Confirmed Suspected

  • Feb 2026: A research count (ICCT/GLOBSEC) puts France second in Europe with 20 Russia-linked incidents since 2022. Claimed
  • Jun 2026: French investigators were reported to be working on several suspected Russia-linked cases, among them railway infrastructure and a Belarus-born man held near Toulouse after filming a military drone prototype. Reported
  • 11–12 Oct 2026: Freezer controls at more than 700 supermarket sites were attacked (a cyber case, listed here because of who is blamed). French authorities suspect Iran's Revolutionary Guard; Paris prosecutors opened a judicial investigation and requested international arrest warrants. Pro-Russian groups also claimed it. Confirmed Claimed
  • Nov 2026: Paris prosecutors are examining whether foreign powers are behind the hoax bomb threats against flights. Confirmed

What it shows: In France the tool is provocation meant to divide people, as much as sabotage.NL – Wat het toont: In Frankrijk is het wapen provocatie om mensen tegen elkaar op te zetten, evenzeer als sabotage.

Germany 8 on record

  • 2025: The federal police chief counted more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights. One Frankfurt shutdown turned out to be a 41-year-old hobby pilot testing a new drone. Confirmed
  • Jul 2026: Fire on the rail line between Düsseldorf and Cologne damaged signal cables; investigated as possible sabotage. No link to any state found. Suspected
  • 4 Aug 2026: Leipzig/Halle Airport: a drone carrying explosives was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane; the charge did not go off. Three drones were found in all. Reports differ on details. Confirmed
  • 11 Aug 2026: A drone forced repeated closures at Hanover Airport; federal police could not stop it with their equipment (Der Spiegel). Reported
  • 1 Sep 2026: The German government formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack ("police investigations, patterns of the act and intelligence findings") and ordered the Russian consulate general in Bonn closed. Russia called it absurd. No arrests found. Confirmed Claimed
  • Sep 2026: A confidential police report, cited by Süddeutsche Zeitung, counts more than 165 suspected acts of sabotage and nearly 750 suspicious drone incidents since January 2026. Reported
  • 28 Oct 2026: Two Belarusian men were arrested in southern Germany, suspected of planning fires near a railway line and a power line for Russia. Romania links them to the Brașov fire. Confirmed Suspected

What it shows: The first case in the EU where a government formally blamed Russia for a drone with explosives at an airport.NL – Wat het toont: De eerste zaak in de EU waarin een regering Rusland formeel de schuld gaf van een drone met explosieven op een luchthaven.

Greece nothing found

What it shows: Three-quarters of the main transatlantic cables pass near a country with almost no means to guard them.NL – Wat het toont: Driekwart van de belangrijkste trans-Atlantische kabels loopt langs een land dat ze nauwelijks kan bewaken.

Poland 10 on record

What it shows: A warning from the intelligence service, without a public case to show.NL – Wat het toont: Een waarschuwing van de inlichtingendienst, zonder publieke zaak om te tonen.

What it shows: Treat the two halves differently. For drones over airports, the lesson of 2025–2026 is better detection and calmer communication, because most alarms could not be proven. For sabotage, the lesson is the opposite: it is real, it is cheap, it is done by hired hands recruited online, and it has moved from fires in shops to arms factories, railways, sea cables and ships.NL – Wat het toont: Behandel de twee helften verschillend. Voor drones boven luchthavens is de les van 2025–2026: betere detectie en rustiger communiceren, want de meeste alarmen konden niet bewezen worden. Voor sabotage is de les omgekeerd: ze is echt, ze is goedkoop, ze wordt uitgevoerd door online geronselde handlangers, en ze is opgeschoven van brandjes in winkels naar wapenfabrieken, spoorwegen, zeekabels en schepen.

  • Not found: the outcome of the Swedish airport investigations, arrests in the Leipzig case, any verdict in Poland's Mika case, who sent the hoax threats.

In plain words · In gewone woorden

The elections of 2025 and 2026 in the other 30 countries: what was faked or attacked, who was blamed, and whether it changed anything.

NL: De verkiezingen van 2025 en 2026 in de andere 30 landen: wat vervalst of aangevallen werd, wie de schuld kreeg, en of het iets veranderde.

Elections and democracy: the other 30 countries

Interference with elections and with the people in politics, in the other 26 EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, 2025 and 2026. 34 events in 14 countries.

In plain words

About a dozen national elections were held in these two years, and in none of them was the counting or the voting itself attacked; most of Europe votes on paper. What was attacked is the talk around the vote. The same two Russian operations, known as Storm-1516 and Matryoshka, turn up in Germany, France, Hungary and Sweden with fake videos about ballot fraud. Party websites were knocked offline in Poland and Norway. But the reports also show three less comfortable things: observers usually found no effect on the result, a good part of the fakes came from inside the country, and in Italy the spyware on critics' phones was the state's own.

NL: In deze twee jaar werden een twaalftal nationale verkiezingen gehouden, en bij geen enkele werd het tellen of het stemmen zelf aangevallen; het grootste deel van Europa stemt op papier. Wat aangevallen werd, is het gesprek rond de stembusgang. Dezelfde twee Russische operaties, bekend als Storm-1516 en Matrjosjka, duiken op in Duitsland, Frankrijk, Hongarije en Zweden met nepvideo's over stembusfraude. Partijwebsites werden platgelegd in Polen en Noorwegen. Maar de rapporten tonen ook drie minder comfortabele dingen: waarnemers vonden meestal geen effect op de uitslag, een flink deel van de vervalsingen kwam van binnen het land, en in Italië was de spyware op de telefoons van critici van de staat zelf.

Labels. Confirmed stated by an authority, a court, observers or named researchers. Reported in the press, not verified. Suspected believed, not proven. Claimed said by one party (a government, a minister, a platform owner) without evidence shown in public. Not proven looked for and not found. Two labels on one line: the first is for the event, the second for who was behind it or whether it had effect.
