Denmark, Latvia, Slovenia, Cyprus, Bulgaria and Ireland also voted or will vote in this period; for them nothing specific about an attack on the election was found, beyond what is on the country cards.

Statements and measures at EU level

  • 15 Dec 2025: the EU put sanctions on John Mark Dougan, an American in Moscow, for running a network of fake news sites and supporting Storm-1516. Confirmed
  • Who runs Storm-1516: European and US authorities attribute it to a Moscow "centre for geopolitical expertise" and to Russian military intelligence; leaked documents reported in 2026 point the same way and also to the Russian presidential administration. Confirmed Claimed
  • Mar 2026: the EU's diplomatic service warned in its yearly report that the elections in Slovenia, Hungary, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Estonia, Sweden, Latvia and Denmark could face the same patterns. Confirmed

Countries with something on record

Bulgaria 1 on record

  • 2025–2026: Websites knocked offline in attacks that authorities and experts attribute to pro-Russian groups; ahead of the 2026 election the government started a programme against disinformation and asked the EU for help. From a US Congress research report. Reported

What it shows: Preparation rather than a recorded attack.NL – Wat het toont: Voorbereiding, geen geregistreerde aanval.

Cyprus 1 on record

  • 13 Nov 2026: The president said he does not rule out interference by artificial intelligence in the next elections: "we are of course all vulnerable". Confirmed

What it shows: A warning, nothing on record yet.NL – Wat het toont: Een waarschuwing, nog niets geregistreerd.

Czechia 2 on record

  • 3–4 Oct 2025: Parliamentary election. Researchers found networks linked to Russia trying to undermine trust in the vote, and clusters of accounts on TikTok, X and Telegram pushing foreign stories, but no operation able to change the result. Confirmed Not proven
  • Autumn 2025: The fact-checker Demagog found hundreds of fake TikTok accounts spreading pro-Russian and anti-establishment content, and no evidence that the network was run from or by Russia. Confirmed Not proven

What it shows: Plenty of noise, no effect found, and the Russian hand not shown.NL – Wat het toont: Veel lawaai, geen effect gevonden, en de Russische hand niet aangetoond.

Denmark 2 on record

  • Nov 2025: Websites were attacked before the local elections. In December Danish military intelligence blamed the pro-Russian group NoName057(16) and linked it to the Russian state. Confirmed Claimed
  • 2026: A Nordic fact-checking network counts 247 attacks by activist-hacker groups on Denmark in 2026; they rise around elections and decisions that go against Russia. Not tied to one election. Reported

What it shows: Websites go down around every vote; the vote itself is on paper.NL – Wat het toont: Websites gaan plat rond elke stembusgang; het stemmen zelf gebeurt op papier.

France 4 on record

  • May 2025: The state agency against foreign digital interference (Viginum) published a technical report on the Russian operation known as Storm-1516. Confirmed
  • 6 Mar 2026: Before the municipal elections France accused Russia over a fake website aimed at a centre-right candidate for mayor of Paris. Viginum said it was probably the Storm-1516 network. It reached few people: under 20,000 views on X. Confirmed Claimed
  • Mar 2026: Viginum also found 28 Facebook pages and 15 French-language websites run from abroad that pushed alarmist AI-made content; it judged the aim to be profit, not politics. A fake audio clip of the mayor of Grenoble was made with free voice-cloning tools. Confirmed
  • 2026: New: the agency published a weekly bulletin on foreign interference during the campaign. Confirmed

What it shows: France now tells voters every week what it sees, and says when a fake is small.NL – Wat het toont: Frankrijk vertelt kiezers nu elke week wat het ziet, en zegt het erbij wanneer een vervalsing klein is.

Germany 4 on record

  • Feb 2025: Federal election, 23 February. Fake videos claimed the AfD party was missing from postal ballots; researchers counted more than 700 fake accounts in the last week. Two days before the vote the government said it had indications of a Russian campaign. Confirmed
  • 12 Dec 2025: The foreign ministry: "We can now state definitively that Russia, through the Storm 1516 campaign, sought to influence and destabilise the most recent federal election." The Russian ambassador was summoned. The same day Germany blamed Russian military intelligence for the 2024 attack on air traffic control. Confirmed Claimed
  • Aug 2026: A deepfake of Chancellor Merz using the stolen logo of Deutsche Welle was attributed to Storm-1516. One technology outlet. Reported
  • Sep 2026: A Russian disinformation campaign was reported ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. One outlet. Reported

What it shows: The only country that has formally blamed a state for interfering in a national election in these two years.NL – Wat het toont: Het enige land dat in deze twee jaar formeel een staat de schuld gaf van inmenging in een nationale verkiezing.

Hungary 5 on record

  • Feb–Mar 2026: TikTok removed two networks of fake accounts; a pro-Kremlin network impersonated Euronews to spread fake reports about the election. Confirmed
  • Mar–Apr 2026: Two Russian operations, Storm-1516 and "Matryoshka", spread fake videos, for example that Hungarian men would be drafted to fight for Ukraine if the opposition won. Analysts add that most of the disinformation in the campaign came from inside Hungary. Confirmed Claimed
  • Spring 2026: An attack on the app of the opposition party Tisza reportedly led to stolen data that was then passed to pro-government media. One source. Reported
  • Spring 2026: The then government declassified part of an intelligence report claiming that IT specialists close to Tisza were linked to Ukraine's volunteer hacker force. The opposition called it a fabrication. Claimed
  • 12 Apr 2026: Election day. International observers: a lively contest with record turnout, but no equal chances because of the ruling party's advantages; several AI-made videos by political actors circulated. The opposition won and formed the government. Confirmed

What it shows: Foreign fakes were there, but the heavier pressure came from inside the country.NL – Wat het toont: Er waren buitenlandse vervalsingen, maar de zwaarste druk kwam van binnen het land.

Italy 2 on record

  • 5 Jun 2025: The parliamentary committee that oversees the secret services confirmed that the government used the spyware Graphite, made by the firm Paragon, against two migration activists, and called that lawful. It found no evidence that the services targeted a journalist whose phone had also been attacked. Confirmed
  • Jun 2025: Researchers at Citizen Lab then confirmed with high confidence that two journalists, one of them Italian, were hit with the same spyware. Paragon ended its contracts with Italy on 9 June, saying Italy refused a check that would have settled who targeted the journalist; Italy disputes that account. Confirmed Suspected

What it shows: Here the state itself used spyware on its critics, and nobody has said who targeted the journalists.NL – Wat het toont: Hier gebruikte de staat zelf spyware tegen zijn critici, en niemand heeft gezegd wie de journalisten viseerde.

Netherlands 2 on record

  • Oct 2025: Before the election of 29 October a newspaper revealed that two members of parliament of the PVV party secretly ran a Facebook page posting hundreds of AI-made images of an opposition leader; the page had 74 million views between June and October. The party leader apologised; the opposition filed a police complaint. Confirmed
  • After the vote: An election observatory found significant digital manipulation, including new AI threats and failing moderation by platforms, and concluded the election was "tested, but fundamentally free and fair". Confirmed

What it shows: The fake images came from sitting members of parliament, not from abroad.NL – Wat het toont: De nepbeelden kwamen van zetelende parlementsleden, niet uit het buitenland.

Norway 1 on record

  • Sep 2025: Parliamentary election. Websites were knocked offline; the security service linked an attack on the website of the Conservative Party to a pro-Russian hacker group. The Swedish psychological-defence agency concludes the attempts had no effect. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: Attempts, no effect.NL – Wat het toont: Pogingen, geen effect.

Poland 3 on record

  • Apr 2025: Prime Minister Tusk said attackers tried for about twelve hours to take over computers of his party's office and campaign staff, and spoke of foreign interference from "the east". Confirmed Claimed
  • 14–16 May 2025: Days before the first round of the presidential election the state research institute NASK found political adverts on Facebook that may have been paid from abroad and that outspent every campaign committee in a week; Meta blocked them. On 16 May Tusk said Russian hackers on Telegram had knocked party websites offline. Confirmed Claimed
  • Jan–Jun 2025: NASK tracked more than 10,000 accounts spreading disinformation; the ministry called the Russian attempts unprecedented. Independent experts found the interference lower than expected, and international observers praised the countermeasures. Confirmed

What it shows: A government that shouted early, and observers who say the defence worked.NL – Wat het toont: Een regering die vroeg alarm sloeg, en waarnemers die zeggen dat de verdediging werkte.

Portugal 1 on record

  • May 2025: During the snap election a false story, dressed up as a CNN report, said Russian state groups had carried out a cyberattack. CNN Portugal denied it. Fact-checkers say much of the false content matched known Russian operations. Confirmed Suspected

What it shows: A fake about an attack that did not happen.NL – Wat het toont: Een vervalsing over een aanval die niet gebeurde.

Romania 5 on record

  • Dec 2024: Background: the constitutional court annulled the first round of the presidential election, citing manipulation of opinion by a foreign state. Moscow denies it. Confirmed
  • 4 May 2025: First round of the rerun. Pro-Russian hackers claimed attacks on government websites, among them the interior and justice ministries. Confirmed Claimed
  • 18–19 May 2025: Run-off, won by the centrist Nicușor Dan. Telegram's founder Pavel Durov sent every Romanian user a message alleging that France had asked him to silence conservative voices; France denies it. Romanian ministries accused Russia of interfering in the run-off. Confirmed Claimed
  • 2025–2026: The European Commission's investigation into TikTok's handling of election risks was still running months later. Confirmed
  • Nov 2026: The candidate barred from the rerun, Călin Georgescu, is on trial in two cases (an attempt against the constitutional order; promoting fascist leaders), has been in pre-trial detention since 29 September and was indicted on 12 November for a €1.1 million fraud. Confirmed Suspected

What it shows: The only annulled national election in the EU; the proof of who steered it has still not been tested in court.NL – Wat het toont: De enige vernietigde nationale verkiezing in de EU; het bewijs van wie ze stuurde is nog altijd niet voor de rechter getoetst.

Sweden 1 on record

  • Sep 2026: Parliamentary election. The pro-Russian "Matryoshka" network spread false claims of election fraud and fabricated videos against the prime minister. The psychological-defence agency said Sweden was not a priority target for Russia; the security service still ranks Russia first for interference. Voting is on paper. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: Fakes about fraud, aimed at trust in the count.NL – Wat het toont: Vervalsingen over fraude, gericht op het vertrouwen in de telling.

Nothing specific found

Austria, Croatia, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Switzerland.

Nothing found means nothing came up in searches on 15 November 2026. Spyware cases in Greece and Spain date from before 2025; the infection of a Greek former member of the European Parliament is on the Belgium page, because it concerns the Parliament.

What it shows: Nobody hacked a ballot box. The attacks are on belief: fake videos saying the count is rigged, fake reports of attacks that never happened. Three lessons stand out from the countries that handled it best. Vote on paper. Tell the public quickly and plainly what you see, including when it is small, as France now does every week. And look at home as well as abroad: in the Netherlands and Hungary, and with Italy's spyware, the source was domestic.NL – Wat het toont: Niemand hackte een stembus. De aanvallen richten zich op het geloof: nepvideo's die zeggen dat de telling vervalst is, nepberichten over aanvallen die nooit gebeurden. Drie lessen vallen op bij de landen die het best reageerden. Stem op papier. Vertel het publiek snel en duidelijk wat je ziet, ook wanneer het klein is, zoals Frankrijk nu elke week doet. En kijk in eigen land evengoed als in het buitenland: in Nederland en Hongarije, en bij de Italiaanse spyware, lag de bron binnenlands.

Europe · Europa
In plain words · In gewone woorden

Military cyber forces, reserves, spending and the rules for acting at home in the other 30 countries, side by side.

NL: Militaire cybertroepen, reserves, uitgaven en de regels om in eigen land op te treden in de andere 30 landen, naast elkaar.

The defence side: the other 30 countries

Military cyber forces, reserves, money and the rules for acting at home, in the other 26 EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, 2025 and 2026. 24 entries in 15 countries.

In plain words

Three things stand out. First, size: Germany has a whole branch of its armed forces for cyber with more than 15,000 people and Poland about 6,500 plus a reserve; most others have a few hundred. Second, the countries nearest to Russia spend far more: Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia and Poland are all above 4.5% of their economy, against about 2% for Belgium, Italy and Portugal. Third, the law is catching up with drones: Germany now lets its army jam or shoot them down at home, France lets the owners of vital sites do it, and Europe is discussing the same for utilities. On cyber help for hospitals and towns, only Estonia has a practised volunteer reserve.

NL: Drie dingen vallen op. Eén, de omvang: Duitsland heeft een hele tak van zijn strijdkrachten voor cyber met meer dan 15.000 mensen en Polen ongeveer 6.500 plus een reserve; de meeste andere hebben er enkele honderden. Twee, de landen het dichtst bij Rusland geven veel meer uit: Litouwen, Estland, Letland en Polen zitten allemaal boven 4,5% van hun economie, tegen ongeveer 2% voor België, Italië en Portugal. Drie, de wet haalt de drones in: Duitsland laat zijn leger ze nu in eigen land storen of neerhalen, Frankrijk laat de eigenaars van vitale sites dat doen, en Europa bespreekt hetzelfde voor nutsbedrijven. Voor cyberhulp aan ziekenhuizen en gemeenten heeft alleen Estland een geoefende vrijwilligersreserve.

Labels. Confirmed stated by a government, an army, NATO or the EU. Reported in the press, not verified. Claimed said by one party without public evidence. Suspected arrested or believed, not judged. Two labels on one line: the first is for the event, the second for a detail or for who was behind it.

Spending on core defence, 2026

NATO estimates published in July 2026, as reported by Reuters: share of the economy spent on core defence. NATO's goal, agreed in The Hague in June 2025, is 3.5% for core defence plus up to 1.5% for wider security such as cybersecurity and vital infrastructure, by 2035.

On 21 October 2026 Reuters reported that Europe is weighing more powers for utilities and infrastructure companies to bring down drones.

At EU and NATO level

  • Eastern Flank Watch, with its "drone wall": approved as a joint project by member states on 28 September 2026, with an indicative €60 to 100 billion up to 2036; twelve member states plus Norway and Ukraine take part; Finland and Poland lead. A first capacity against drones is promised for the end of 2026 and full operation for 2027–2028. Critics say that so far it is mostly a budget line. Confirmed Claimed
  • Attacks on the arms industry: the EU institutions' own cyber team reported a suspected Russia-linked campaign against European defence companies in August 2026; the French defence group Thales confirmed a data leak through an outside firm in May 2026. Confirmed Suspected

Countries with something on record

Denmark 1 on record

  • Oct 2025: After the drone reports Denmark banned all civilian drone flights for the days when European leaders met in Copenhagen. Confirmed

What it shows: A ban on flying, not a rule for shooting.NL – Wat het toont: Een vliegverbod, geen regel om te schieten.

Estonia 2 on record

  • 2025–2026: The army's Cyber Command has about 300 people. Behind it stands the cyber unit of the volunteer Defence League, staffed by IT professionals; in wartime the command would grow to about four times its size from that pool. A separate civilian cyber reserve of the state IT authority has held five exercises with operators of vital services, the latest at Tallinn Airport. Confirmed
  • 2026: Estonia spends an estimated 5.1% of its economy on core defence. Confirmed

What it shows: The model others look at: volunteers from the IT sector, practised every year.NL – Wat het toont: Het model waar anderen naar kijken: vrijwilligers uit de IT-sector, die elk jaar oefenen.

Finland 2 on record

  • Dec 2025: Finland and Poland announced that they will jointly lead the EU project to guard the eastern border (Eastern Flank Watch). Confirmed
  • Jan–Apr 2026: A break-in at the phone-management service of the state IT centre Valtori reportedly exposed data on military officers, diplomats and counter-terrorism staff; police widened the investigation in April. Confirmed Reported

What it shows: Even here the soldiers' data leaked through an office service, not through the army.NL – Wat het toont: Zelfs hier lekten de gegevens van militairen via een kantoordienst, niet via het leger.

France 3 on record

  • 2025–2030: The army is building a Cyber Defence Regiment that will reach 400 people from the three services by 2030, next to its cyber command. Confirmed
  • Aug (year not confirmed): Parliament passed a law letting approved operators of vital infrastructure and their contractors detect, jam and shoot down drones near designated sites. Reported in October 2026. Reported
  • 2026: An estimated 2.22% of the economy on core defence. Confirmed

What it shows: The first country to let the owners of power plants and airports bring down drones themselves.NL – Wat het toont: Het eerste land dat de eigenaars van centrales en luchthavens zelf drones laat neerhalen.

Germany 3 on record

  • Jun 2025: The Cyber and Information Domain Service, a full branch of the armed forces, counted 15,659 people. Confirmed
  • 26 Feb 2026: Parliament changed the aviation security law: the armed forces may jam or shoot down drones when a state asks for help, and the defence ministry decides alone. Flying a drone into an airport's security zone became a crime. Confirmed
  • 2026: An estimated 2.69% of the economy on core defence. Confirmed

What it shows: By far the largest military cyber branch in the EU, and now a legal basis to shoot at drones at home.NL – Wat het toont: Veruit de grootste militaire cybertak in de EU, en nu een wettelijke basis om in eigen land op drones te schieten.

Greece 3 on record

  • 5 Feb 2026: A high-ranking military officer was arrested on espionage charges; for whom is not stated in the reports found. Confirmed Suspected
  • Apr 2026: Reuters reported that Russia-linked hackers broke into 27 email accounts of the Hellenic National Defence General Staff, part of a wider campaign whose main target was Ukraine. The General Staff did not answer questions. Less established outlets name the Russian military-intelligence group APT28. Reported Claimed
  • 2026: An estimated 3.65% of the economy on core defence. Confirmed

What it shows: The one EU army whose own mailboxes are reported broken into in these two years.NL – Wat het toont: Het enige EU-leger waarvan de eigen mailboxen in deze twee jaar gekraakt zouden zijn.

Italy 1 on record

  • 2026: A proposal for a national military cyber body: 1,200 to 1,500 people at first, growing to 5,000 including reservists. An estimated 2.1% of the economy on core defence. Reported

What it shows: A plan on paper.NL – Wat het toont: Een plan op papier.

Latvia 1 on record

  • 2026: An estimated 4.92% of the economy on core defence. The July 2026 draft drew a record 1,560 volunteers; the aim is 4,000 conscripts a year by 2028. Confirmed

What it shows: Money and conscripts, no separate cyber figure found.NL – Wat het toont: Geld en dienstplichtigen, geen apart cybercijfer gevonden.

Lithuania 1 on record

  • 2026: The highest spender in NATO: an estimated 5.33% of the economy on core defence. 5,000 conscripts are called up for 2026, with new cyber training. Lithuania is named among the countries that passed a law on bringing down drones; no details found. It has no civilian volunteer cyber reserve. Confirmed Reported

What it shows: The biggest budget, but no volunteer cyber reserve like Estonia's.NL – Wat het toont: Het grootste budget, maar geen vrijwillige cyberreserve zoals die van Estland.

Netherlands 1 on record

  • 2025–2026: The defence cyber strategy of 2025 treats cyber as a military domain in its own right; a defence cyber academy is being set up and recruitment for the cyber command is a priority. The Netherlands commits to NATO's 3.5% for core defence only, not to the extra 1.5%. Confirmed

What it shows: Building the school before the force.NL – Wat het toont: Eerst de school bouwen, dan de strijdmacht.

Norway 1 on record

  • 2026: Norway takes part in the EU's Eastern Flank Watch and commits to the 3.5% for core defence only. Confirmed

What it shows: In the EU project without being in the EU.NL – Wat het toont: In het EU-project zonder in de EU te zitten.

Poland 2 on record

  • 2026: About 6,500 people in the Cyberspace Defence Forces, with defensive, reconnaissance and offensive tasks, plus a reserve called the Cyber Legion of around 3,000 (ministry, February 2026). Confirmed
  • 2026: An estimated 4.68% of the economy on core defence. Poland co-leads Eastern Flank Watch and says it wants a working drone wall within three months, a national timetable. Confirmed Claimed

What it shows: A cyber army of thousands with a reserve half its size.NL – Wat het toont: Een cyberleger van duizenden met een reserve die half zo groot is.

Portugal 1 on record

  • 2026: An estimated 2.1% of the economy on core defence. Nothing specific on cyber forces found. Confirmed

What it shows: Only the spending figure.NL – Wat het toont: Alleen het uitgavencijfer.

Romania 1 on record

  • 2025: The president signed a law allowing troops to shoot down drones in Romanian airspace. Date taken from a headline. Reported

What it shows: A law made for drones that stray in from the war next door.NL – Wat het toont: Een wet gemaakt voor drones die uit de oorlog ernaast binnendwalen.

Spain 1 on record

  • 2 Feb 2026: The Joint Cyberspace Command presented a growth plan: 1,500 people by 2030, three times its present strength. Confirmed

What it shows: Tripling in four years, from a small base.NL – Wat het toont: Verdrievoudigen in vier jaar, vanaf een kleine basis.

Nothing specific found

Austria, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Malta, Slovakia, Slovenia, Sweden, Switzerland.

Nothing found means the searches of 16 November 2026 gave no figure or event for the country's military cyber side; several of these countries are neutral or not in NATO. Sweden and Finland have volunteer units, but no numbers were found.

What it shows: Armies are getting money and, slowly, the legal right to act at home, first of all against drones. What almost nobody has is the bridge to civilian life that Estonia built years ago: IT people who volunteer, train with the airport and the hospital every year, and are called when it goes wrong. That costs little compared with air defence, and it is the part that would have helped in most of the attacks in this file.NL – Wat het toont: Legers krijgen geld en, langzaam, het wettelijke recht om in eigen land op te treden, in de eerste plaats tegen drones. Wat bijna niemand heeft, is de brug naar het burgerleven die Estland jaren geleden bouwde: IT'ers die zich vrijwillig melden, elk jaar oefenen met de luchthaven en het ziekenhuis, en opgeroepen worden als het misgaat. Dat kost weinig in vergelijking met luchtverdediging, en het is het deel dat bij de meeste aanvallen in dit dossier geholpen zou hebben.

Europe · Europa
In plain words · In gewone woorden

Which governments want the police to be able to read private messages and which refuse, and the national laws that went further than the EU one.

NL: Welke regeringen willen dat de politie priveberichten kan lezen en welke weigeren, en de nationale wetten die verder gingen dan de Europese.

Encryption and "chat control": the other 30 countries

Where each country stands on letting the police read private messages, and the national laws that go further than the EU one. 26 entries in 18 countries.

In plain words

Europe split in two over this, and the split does not follow the usual lines. A group led by Germany, with Poland, Austria, the Netherlands, Finland, Estonia, Czechia, Slovenia and Luxembourg, blocked the compulsory scanning in the autumn of 2025, and Denmark, which held the presidency, dropped it. France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Ireland, Hungary and Cyprus are named on the other side, Belgium nowhere. Meanwhile two countries tried on their own what the EU could not agree: Sweden with a bill that would make messaging services keep messages, and France with an article that would add the police as a hidden reader. The French article was taken out by its own parliament. What Sweden decided could not be established.

NL: Europa viel hierover in twee, en de breuklijn volgt niet de gewone lijnen. Een groep onder leiding van Duitsland, met Polen, Oostenrijk, Nederland, Finland, Estland, Tsjechië, Slovenië en Luxemburg, blokkeerde in het najaar van 2025 de verplichte scanning, en Denemarken, dat het voorzitterschap had, liet ze vallen. Frankrijk, Spanje, Italië, Portugal, Ierland, Hongarije en Cyprus worden aan de andere kant genoemd, België nergens. Intussen probeerden twee landen op eigen houtje wat de EU niet eens raakte: Zweden met een wetsvoorstel dat berichtendiensten berichten zou doen bewaren, en Frankrijk met een artikel dat de politie als verborgen meelezer zou toevoegen. Het Franse artikel werd door het eigen parlement geschrapt. Wat Zweden besliste, kon niet worden vastgesteld.

Read the country lists with care. There is no official published list of how each government stands. Everything below comes from campaign trackers and press reports, and they contradict each other: Italy appears on both sides, the number of opposing countries is given as five, six, seven or nine depending on the tracker and the date, and positions changed between meetings. Only the statements made in a government’s own words are marked Confirmed here. NL – Lees de landenlijsten met zorg. Er is geen officiële gepubliceerde lijst van hoe elke regering staat. Alles hieronder komt van actiegroepen en persberichten, en die spreken elkaar tegen. Alleen uitspraken in de eigen woorden van een regering staan hier als bevestigd.

Where countries are said to stand

PositionCountries namedHow firm

ForFrance, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Ireland, Hungary, CyprusReported; no government statement found for any of them

What countries tried on their own

CountryWhat it would doWhere it ended
SwedenOblige messaging services to keep messages and give police access to a suspect’s history; in force from 1 March 2026 as proposedSignal said it would leave the country; the armed forces opposed it; the outcome in parliament was not found
FranceArticle 8 ter: oblige messaging services to open access to intercepted conversations, by adding a hidden readerDeleted by the National Assembly’s law commission; attempts to restore it rejected on 20 March 2025

What the courts decided

  • EncroChat, 30 April 2024. The EU Court of Justice, sitting as a Grand Chamber, ruled in case C-670/22 on three points. A prosecutor may ask another member state for data from a cracked encrypted phone network without a judge’s order. The law of the country handing over the evidence is the test for whether it was lawfully obtained. The accused must be able to challenge the evidence for it to be used. It is the ruling every national court now works from. Confirmed
  • Belgium, Sky ECC. The Antwerp court of appeal and the Court of Cassation rejected the procedural challenges; 1,206 convictions. See the Belgium page. Confirmed
  • Germany and the Netherlands. Both had EncroChat cases that reached their highest courts; what those courts held after the EU ruling was not found. Not found

Countries with something on record

Austria 1 on record

  • 2025: Named in every count of the countries blocking the scanning duty. Reported

What it shows: Against, by all accounts.NL – Wat het toont: Tegen, volgens alle tellingen.

Cyprus 1 on record

  • 2025: Named in some counts as a supporter. Cyprus held the presidency for one round of the talks in June 2026. Reported

What it shows: Reported as for.NL – Wat het toont: Gemeld als voor.

Czechia 1 on record

  • Sep 2025: Prime Minister Petr Fiala said in public that Prague would not support the monitoring of citizens’ private correspondence. One of the few positions stated by a head of government in his own words. Confirmed

What it shows: The clearest "no" from the top of a government.NL – Wat het toont: Het duidelijkste "nee" van de top van een regering.

Denmark 2 on record

  • Oct 2025: Holding the EU presidency, Denmark dropped the compulsory scanning from its compromise. Justice Minister Peter Hummelgaard said the screening would stay voluntary. It did so after a blocking minority formed, Germany among them. Confirmed
  • Nov 2025 – 2026: Campaigners disagree whether this was a withdrawal or a pause: the Council kept a permanent voluntary regime in its position, and the talks went on. Claimed

What it shows: The country that had to give way, and the one most accused of trying again.NL – Wat het toont: Het land dat moest toegeven, en dat het meest beschuldigd wordt van een nieuwe poging.

Estonia 1 on record

  • 2025: Named among the opposing countries. Reported

What it shows: Against.NL – Wat het toont: Tegen.

Finland 1 on record

  • 2025: Named among the opposing countries. Reported

What it shows: Against.NL – Wat het toont: Tegen.

France 4 on record

  • Feb–Mar 2025: In the law against drug trafficking the Senate inserted article 8 ter, obliging messaging services to give access to intercepted conversations. Critics, including people inside the government, called it worse than a back door, because the police would be added as a hidden extra reader in a conversation. The interior minister denied it was a back door. The law commission of the National Assembly deleted the article, and on 20 March the Assembly rejected the amendments that tried to put it back. Confirmed
  • 12–13 Jun 2025: The Constitutional Council struck down six provisions of the law (decision 2025-885 DC) and the law was promulgated on 13 June 2025 as law 2025-532. Whether the encryption article appears anywhere in the final text could not be verified in the sources found; the Assembly had removed it. Confirmed Not proven
  • 17 Nov 2026: The National Assembly adopted the "résilience" bill in first reading by 464 votes to 64 with 16 abstentions, according to specialist press. MPs deleted article 16 bis, added by the Senate, on encrypted messaging, by 69 votes to 37 (AEF info; this split is not cross-checked elsewhere). The bill transposes the NIS2 and CER directives; reports differ on how many entities it covers (about 15,000, or more than 18,000 according to the government). A joint Senate-Assembly committee (CMP) is still to come. Confirmed
  • 2025–2026: France is named in most counts as a supporter of the EU scanning duty. Reported

What it shows: A country that pushes for access in Europe and refused it at home, within four months.NL – Wat het toont: Een land dat in Europa toegang bepleit en ze thuis weigerde, binnen vier maanden.

Germany 2 on record

  • Sep–Oct 2025: Germany joined the opposition and forced the Council vote to be delayed. The interior ministry said it could not support measures that break encryption; Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig said chat control without cause must be taboo in a state under the rule of law. Confirmed
  • 2026: One campaign tracker reports that the instructions given to German negotiators since June 2026 no longer rule out a compulsory detection that would supplement the voluntary scanning. Not confirmed elsewhere. Claimed

What it shows: The weight that stopped it, and the position most often said to be shifting.NL – Wat het toont: Het gewicht dat het tegenhield, en de positie waarvan het vaakst gezegd wordt dat ze schuift.

Hungary 1 on record

  • 2025: Named in some counts as a supporter. Reported

What it shows: Reported as for, no statement found.NL – Wat het toont: Gemeld als voor, geen verklaring gevonden.

Ireland 1 on record

  • 2025: Named in some counts as a supporter. Ireland hosts the European headquarters of the largest messaging companies, so the duty would be enforced there. Reported

What it shows: Where the law would actually land.NL – Wat het toont: Waar de wet echt zou neerkomen.

Italy 1 on record

  • 2025–2026: The counts contradict each other: one lists Italy among the formal opponents in June 2026, others among the supporters. No Italian government statement was found. Claimed

What it shows: The clearest example of why these lists should be read with care.NL – Wat het toont: Het duidelijkste voorbeeld waarom deze lijstjes met zorg gelezen moeten worden.

Luxembourg 1 on record

  • Sep–Oct 2025: Joined the opposition together with Germany, which helped create the blocking minority. Reported

What it shows: A small vote that mattered.NL – Wat het toont: Een kleine stem die telde.

Netherlands 1 on record

  • 2025: Named among the opposing countries, after a period of being undecided. One later count lists it among the four formal opponents. Reported

What it shows: Against, after hesitating.NL – Wat het toont: Tegen, na aarzelen.

Poland 1 on record

  • 2023–2025: Reported to have opposed the scanning duty since it was proposed, and to have kept that position across a change of government. Reported

What it shows: The only position said to have survived a change of government.NL – Wat het toont: De enige positie waarvan gezegd wordt dat ze een regeringswissel overleefde.

Portugal 1 on record

  • 2025: Named in some counts as a supporter. Reported

What it shows: Reported as for.NL – Wat het toont: Gemeld als voor.

Slovenia 1 on record

  • 2025: Named among the opposing countries. Reported

What it shows: Against.NL – Wat het toont: Tegen.

Spain 1 on record

  • 2025: Named in most counts as one of the strongest supporters of the scanning duty. Reported

What it shows: Reported as the firmest "yes".NL – Wat het toont: Gemeld als het stevigste "ja".

Sweden 4 on record

  • Feb 2025 – 2026: A bill on data storage and access to electronic information would oblige messaging services such as Signal and WhatsApp to keep messages and give the police access to a suspect’s history. The government wanted it in force on 1 March 2026. Confirmed
  • Feb–Apr 2025: Signal said it would leave Sweden rather than comply, because the change would weaken its whole network. The Global Encryption Coalition wrote to parliament warning the same. Confirmed
  • 2025: The Swedish Armed Forces opposed the bill, warning that such an access mechanism could be used by people it was not meant for. Their own chief information officer had told staff to use Signal for calls and messages that do not concern classified information. The justice minister, the security service and the national police backed the bill. Confirmed
  • 2026: What parliament finally decided could not be established in the sources found. Not proven

What it shows: The one country whose own army said in public that the bill would make it less safe.NL – Wat het toont: Het enige land waarvan het eigen leger publiek zei dat het wetsvoorstel het onveiliger zou maken.

Nothing specific found

Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Iceland, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Malta, Norway, Romania, Slovakia, Switzerland.

Four of these are not in the EU and have no vote on the regulation: Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. For the others, no position and no national law on encryption came up in the searches of 16 November 2026.

What it shows: The argument is not between countries that care about children and countries that care about privacy. It is between those who believe a door can be built for the police alone, and those who do not. The most telling voice is not a privacy group: it is the Swedish army, which told its own government that the law would make the country less safe, having already told its own staff to use the app the law would weaken.NL – Wat het toont: De discussie gaat niet tussen landen die om kinderen geven en landen die om privacy geven. Ze gaat tussen wie gelooft dat je een deur kunt bouwen voor alleen de politie, en wie niet. De veelzeggendste stem is geen privacygroep: het is het Zweedse leger, dat zijn eigen regering zei dat de wet het land onveiliger zou maken, nadat het zijn eigen personeel al had aangeraden de app te gebruiken die de wet zou verzwakken.

Still open

  • What the Swedish parliament decided about the data storage bill.
  • Whether the French encryption article survived anywhere in the promulgated law of 13 June 2025.
  • Whether a seventh round of EU talks happened, and with what result.
  • Any official list of national positions: none is published.
  • What the German and Dutch supreme courts held on EncroChat after the EU ruling.
  • Whether Germany’s position has really shifted since June 2026, as one tracker says.

Europe · Europa
In plain words · In gewone woorden

The attacks that should never have happened: factory passwords left in place, no second lock on the login, warnings nobody acted on. For each one: who was responsible for closing the door.

NL: De aanvallen die nooit hadden mogen gebeuren: fabriekswachtwoorden die bleven staan, geen tweede slot op de login, waarschuwingen waar niemand iets mee deed. Telkens: wie verantwoordelijk was om de deur dicht te doen.

3 · Avoidable failures, and who is accountable

Most of these attacks did not need genius. They walked through doors left open. Each case below is documented, together with who was responsible for closing the door.

Precision matters. Reports say the freezer attackers "tested default administrative credentials". No source we found publishes the exact password, so the accurate wording is "factory passwords" rather than quote a string like "admin12345".

Warned, and still hit

Supermarket freezers

Controllers were connected straight to the internet, with no VPN, on factory login settings. Many were old models the vendor no longer updates. CERT-FR warned on 12 Oct and the CCB on 13 Oct; Counts of exposed systems in Belgium differ by method: Censys found 138, Approach Cyber reportedly about 700, and Brussels Times reported about 970 Danfoss and 123 Copeland systems. The safe word is "hundreds". Belgian stores were hit on 2 Nov.

Anyone with an internet scanner could find them.

In plain words: Freezer computers were left on the internet with factory settings; criminals logged in and turned the heat up.NL – In gewone woorden: De computers van de diepvriezers hingen met fabrieksinstellingen aan het internet; criminelen logden in en zetten de verwarming hoger.

What would have stopped it: Taking them off the open internet, or putting them behind a VPN, after the 13 October warning.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: Ze na de waarschuwing van 13 oktober van het open internet halen, of achter een VPN zetten.

Who had to close the door
  • Store operator and chain HQ: owns the equipment and its risk.
  • Installer or maintenance contractor: set up remote access and left it open.
  • Vendor: shipped default logins and stopped updates on units still in service.
  • The law today: NIS2 covers food wholesale and industrial processing, not supermarket retail. The Cyber Resilience Act's main rules apply only from Dec 2027 and only to new products. Today almost no one is legally obliged to fix this.
The front gate without a lock

FortiBleed firewalls

Firewalls exist to keep attackers out. In 270+ Belgian organisations they became the way in. None of the firewalls examined had multi-factor login switched on. Four months later, attackers still held admin rights on more than 100 of them.

In plain words: The digital front gate opened with a stolen password alone.NL – In gewone woorden: De digitale voordeur ging open met alleen een gestolen wachtwoord.

What would have stopped it: Two-step login, which costs almost nothing.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: Tweestapsverificatie, die bijna niets kost.

Who had to close the door
  • Each organisation's management, personally accountable under NIS2 where it applies.
  • IT service providers that configured and managed the firewalls.
  • Vendor: MFA available but not enforced by default.
Basic techniques, real victims

AI agents found the same open doors

Anthropic said its AI models reached three real organisations using "basic techniques, like accessing unauthenticated endpoints and exploiting weak passwords". None of the three noticed until told. The OpenAI agents got in partly through a customer who had left an interface open that "let anyone run code".

In plain words: Test AI programs walked through weak passwords and open interfaces at real companies.NL – In gewone woorden: AI-programma's in een test wandelden via zwakke wachtwoorden en open toegangen binnen bij echte bedrijven.

What would have stopped it: Strong passwords, closed interfaces, and monitoring that notices strangers.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: Sterke wachtwoorden, gesloten toegangen en bewaking die vreemden opmerkt.

The lesson
  • Weak passwords are no longer found only by patient humans. Automated agents find them in hours.
  • Organisations that don't monitor their systems don't even know they were entered.
One key, 30 institutions

European Commission, Europa.eu

A single compromised AWS cloud credential, obtained through a poisoned security tool (Trivy), exposed website data of the Commission and 29 other EU bodies. It was leaked online four days later.

In plain words: One stolen digital key opened data of 30 EU bodies.NL – In gewone woorden: Eén gestolen digitale sleutel opende gegevens van 30 EU-instellingen.

What would have stopped it: Splitting access so one key can't open everything, and checking security tools themselves.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: Toegang opsplitsen zodat één sleutel niet alles opent, en de beveiligingstools zelf controleren.

Accountability
  • The Commission as data controller.
  • Supply-chain risk in "trusted" security tools.
  • One credential should never unlock that much.
Storing the keys to people's phones

Orange Belgium

850,000 customers' PUK codes and SIM identifiers were exposed. Those are exactly what a criminal needs to hijack a phone number and then reset bank and email logins.

In plain words: The unlock codes of 850,000 SIM cards were stored where a breach could reach them.NL – In gewone woorden: De ontgrendelcodes van 850.000 simkaarten stonden waar een inbraak ze kon bereiken.

What would have stopped it: Not storing PUK codes where attackers can get at them, and extra checks before any SIM swap.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: PUK-codes niet bewaren waar aanvallers erbij kunnen, en extra controles voor elke simwissel.

Accountability
  • Telecom operator under GDPR and telecom law.
  • Should PUK codes be stored where a breach can reach them at all?
One email was enough

Phishing still opens town halls and schools

Machelen (Sep 2026) went down after phishing; IHECS was believed to start the same way. At ULB, staff login credentials were found exposed. Strong logins that resist phishing stop most of these.

In plain words: One fake email gave criminals a way in.NL – In gewone woorden: Eén valse e-mail gaf criminelen een weg naar binnen.

What would have stopped it: Phishing-resistant logins and training staff to report, not click.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: Aanmeldingen die bestand zijn tegen phishing, en personeel dat leert melden in plaats van klikken.

Accountability
  • Local and school management.
  • Regions and federations that fund their IT without setting minimum standards.
Known weak, still weak

Hospitals and local government

Three in four hospitals were below the required cyber level in January 2026, despite €105M invested since 2022. A Flemish audit (as reported) found no ICT continuity plan at 59% of the local authorities examined. Then AZ Monica needed about five weeks to get its main systems back.

In plain words: Known weaknesses stayed unfixed for years.NL – In gewone woorden: Gekende zwakke plekken bleven jarenlang onopgelost.

What would have stopped it: Funding tied to fixing them, drills, and shared security services.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: Geld gekoppeld aan het oplossen ervan, oefeningen en gedeelde beveiligingsdiensten.

Accountability
  • Hospital boards (NIS2 essential entities, deadline 18 Apr 2026).
  • Mayors and councils as owners of municipal IT.
Repeat offenders

Security vendors as the weak link

Ivanti (Commission, VSSE, Dutch watchdog, Finnish state IT), Fortinet (FortiBleed), Barracuda (VSSE before). The products bought to protect are among the most exploited entry points in Europe. Ahold Delhaize had its second major incident in two years.

In plain words: The products bought for protection had holes that were exploited.NL – In gewone woorden: De producten die gekocht werden ter bescherming hadden lekken die misbruikt werden.

What would have stopped it: Vendor liability, certification and fixed patch deadlines.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: Aansprakelijkheid van leveranciers, certificering en vaste termijnen om lekken te dichten.

Accountability
  • Vendors face almost no liability today.
  • Buyers keep choosing them without contractual security guarantees.
One supplier down, a sector down

Single points of failure

Collins Aerospace hit several European airports. ChipSoft serves about 70% of Dutch hospitals. One shared web host took 300+ Belgian municipal sites down. Danfoss controllers run cold chains across Europe.

In plain words: One supplier went down and a whole sector stopped.NL – In gewone woorden: Eén leverancier viel uit en een hele sector lag stil.

What would have stopped it: A tested fallback and an exit plan for every critical supplier.NL – Wat het had tegengehouden: Een geteste noodoplossing en een vertrekplan voor elke kritieke leverancier.

Accountability
  • Sector regulators who never mapped these dependencies.
  • Buyers who accepted no exit or fallback plan.

Proof that defence works when it is done properly: police operations, arrests, money frozen, and attacks that failed.

NL: Bewijs dat verdediging werkt als ze goed gebeurt: politieoperaties, arrestaties, bevroren geld, en aanvallen die mislukten.

Good news: defence works when it's done

Most of this file is alarming. These cases show that action pays off.

  1. Jul 2025
    Europol's Operation Eastwood against NoName057(16)

    The pro-Russian group behind the DDoS attacks on Belgian websites: 12 countries took part, more than 100 servers were taken down or disrupted, 2 arrests (France, Spain), 7 European arrest warrants and 24 searches.

    Why it matters: The group that knocks Belgian websites offline lost most of its computers in one coordinated police action.NL – Waarom het telt: De groep die Belgische websites platlegt, verloor in één gecoördineerde politieactie het grootste deel van zijn computers.

  2. 2025
    Belgian police help arrest 8Base ransomware leaders

    Four key figures arrested in a Europol operation with 14 countries, Belgian federal police among them.

    Why it matters: Belgian investigators helped catch the leaders of a gang that locked companies' files for ransom.NL – Waarom het telt: Belgische speurders hielpen de leiders oppakken van een bende die bedrijfsbestanden gijzelde voor losgeld.

  3. Brussels
    First Belgian trial of Russian ransomware suspects

    Two Russians arrested in Spain in 2023 and extradited to Belgium; 16 servers seized. The federal prosecutor called it the first such trial in the country.

    Why it matters: Russian hackers were brought before a Belgian judge for the first time. Distance isn't always protection for criminals.NL – Waarom het telt: Russische hackers stonden voor het eerst voor een Belgische rechter. Afstand beschermt criminelen niet altijd.

  4. Sep 2025
    Arrest after the Brussels Airport attack

    The UK's National Crime Agency arrested a man in his 40s within days.

    Why it matters: Within days of the airport chaos, police arrested a suspect.NL – Waarom het telt: Enkele dagen na de chaos op de luchthaven pakte de politie een verdachte op.

  5. Dec 2025 → Jul 2026
    Poland's grid attack failed, and was punished

    The wiper attack on about 30 energy sites failed. Seven months later the EU and the UK named a unit of Russia's FSB security service (Centre 16) and imposed their first coordinated cyber sanctions.

    Why it matters: The attack didn't cut the power, and Europe named and sanctioned those responsible.NL – Waarom het telt: De aanval zette de stroom niet af, en Europa noemde en bestrafte de verantwoordelijken.

  6. Oct 2026
    FPS Finance stopped its attacker within hours

    No data taken, services restored, deadline extended for citizens. A model response.

    Why it matters: Our tax administration spotted the intruder fast, shut the doors, and lost no data, by its own account.NL – Waarom het telt: Onze belastingadministratie zag de indringer snel, sloot de deuren en verloor volgens eigen zeggen geen gegevens.

  7. Ongoing
    Banks stop most phishing transfers

    Febelfin: 75% of transfers made after phishing are still detected, blocked or recovered.

    Why it matters: If you call your bank immediately, there's a good chance your money comes back.NL – Waarom het telt: Als je je bank meteen belt, is er een goede kans dat je je geld terugkrijgt.

  8. Jul 2026
    Deepfake fraud gang dismantled

    Five arrests after more than 200 Belgians were defrauded.

    Why it matters: The people behind fake celebrity investment ads were caught.NL – Waarom het telt: De mensen achter valse beleggingsadvertenties met bekende gezichten werden opgepakt.

  9. Oct–Nov 2026
    Fast money freezes and fast attribution

    About $3 billion of the Binance theft was frozen within days. France named the IRGC unit behind its freezer attacks within four weeks.

    Why it matters: Half of the biggest crypto theft ever was frozen before criminals could use it.NL – Waarom het telt: De helft van de grootste cryptodiefstal ooit werd bevroren voor criminelen ze konden gebruiken.

EN

Laws and what comes next · Wetten en wat volgt
In plain words · In gewone woorden

Which rules Europe and Belgium already have against cyberattacks, which ones are being written now, and which are planned. Each law is explained from scratch: who must do what, since when, what happens if they don't, and where it fell short this year.

NL: Welke regels Europa en België al hebben tegen cyberaanvallen, welke nu geschreven worden, en welke gepland zijn. Elke wet wordt van nul uitgelegd: wie wat moet doen, sinds wanneer, wat er gebeurt als ze het niet doen, en waar ze dit jaar tekortschoot.

Laws and regulations: what the EU and Belgium do

Everything that is in place, everything being negotiated and everything planned, explained from the ground up. Read it once from top to bottom; afterwards the one-minute picture is enough.

The picture in one minute

In plain words

Think of road safety. There are rules for drivers, safety standards for cars, an inspectorate, an ambulance service, and penalties for those who cause accidents on purpose. Europe's cyber rules follow the same pattern. Rules for organisations: NIS2 obliges hospitals, energy companies and other vital organisations to protect themselves. Standards for products: the Cyber Resilience Act says every connected device must be safe when sold. The inspectorate and the label: the Cybersecurity Act created the European agency ENISA and security certificates. The ambulance: the Cyber Solidarity Act provides an emergency team. The penalties: sanctions against foreign attackers. Belgium turns the European rules into national law and runs its own cyber centre, the CCB. What is missing shows in this autumn's attacks: some organisations and millions of existing devices fall outside the rules, and a warning obliges nobody to act.

NL: Denk aan verkeersveiligheid. Er zijn regels voor bestuurders, veiligheidsnormen voor auto's, een inspectie, een ambulancedienst, en straffen voor wie met opzet ongelukken veroorzaakt. De Europese cyberregels volgen hetzelfde patroon. Regels voor organisaties: NIS2 verplicht ziekenhuizen, energiebedrijven en andere vitale organisaties om zich te beschermen. Normen voor producten: de Cyber Resilience Act zegt dat elk verbonden toestel veilig moet zijn bij verkoop. De inspectie en het label: de Cybersecurity Act creëerde het Europese agentschap ENISA en veiligheidscertificaten. De ambulance: de Cyber Solidarity Act zorgt voor een noodploeg. De straffen: sancties tegen buitenlandse aanvallers. België zet de Europese regels om in nationale wetten en heeft een eigen cybercentrum, het CCB. Wat ontbreekt, bleek dit najaar: sommige organisaties en miljoenen bestaande toestellen vallen buiten de regels, en een waarschuwing verplicht niemand om iets te doen.

How a European law is made, in plain words

  • Two kinds of law. A regulation applies directly and identically in all 27 countries (the Cyber Resilience Act). A directive sets a goal, and each country writes its own national law to reach it (NIS2). That is why NIS2 applies in Belgium since 2024 but still not fully in France or Spain.
  • Who decides. The European Commission proposes. The European Parliament and the Council (the 27 governments) must both agree on the same text.
  • Inside Parliament. A committee does the work. For cyber and energy that is ITRE. One member, the rapporteur, writes a draft report; the others table amendments; the committee votes; then the whole Parliament votes.
  • The final stretch. Parliament, Council and Commission negotiate a common text behind closed doors. From proposal to law usually takes one and a half to two years. After that come the detailed technical rules, and for a directive the national laws.
  • What a member can do. Table amendments, negotiate compromises for a political group, question the Commission, and vote.

The European laws in force

aNIS2: the law for vital organisations · NIS2: de wet voor vitale organisaties

Status: EU directive 2022/2555. Countries had to turn it into national law by 17 October 2024. Belgium did so on time.

In plain words: NIS2 tells the organisations a country cannot do without (hospitals, energy, water, transport, banks, the digital backbone, public administration and more) that they must protect their computer systems, and that they must report a serious attack quickly. It is to cybersecurity what fire-safety rules are to buildings: you must have the extinguishers and the escape plan, and an inspector can check.

NL: NIS2 zegt tegen de organisaties die een land niet kan missen (ziekenhuizen, energie, water, vervoer, banken, de digitale ruggengraat, de overheid en meer) dat ze hun computersystemen moeten beschermen en een ernstige aanval snel moeten melden. Het is voor cyberveiligheid wat brandveiligheidsregels voor gebouwen zijn: je moet de blussers en het vluchtplan hebben, en een inspecteur kan het controleren.

  • Who: 18 sectors. Large organisations in the most vital sectors are "essential"; the others are "important". As a rule it applies from 50 employees or €10 million turnover; some organisations are covered whatever their size.
  • What they must do: ten basic measures, among them a risk analysis, a plan to keep working during an attack, backups, checking their suppliers, staff training, and two-step login.
  • Reporting: a first warning within 24 hours of a serious incident, a fuller report within 72 hours, a final report within a month.
  • Who answers for it: the board or management personally approves the measures and can be held liable.
  • Fines: up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide turnover for essential organisations; up to €7 million or 1.4% for important ones.
  • How Europe enforces it on countries: on 8 July 2026 the Commission took Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice for still not having turned NIS2 into national law.

Where it fell short in 2026: Supermarket retail is not covered, so nobody was legally obliged to secure the freezers. Small firms that manage thousands of devices for others fall below the size threshold. A warning from the cyber centre carries no deadline. And four large countries were still not applying the law at all.

bCyber Resilience Act: the law for safe products · Cyber Resilience Act: de wet voor veilige producten

Status: EU regulation 2024/2847, in force. Reporting duties apply since 11 September 2026; the main rules from 11 December 2027.

In plain words: NIS2 is about organisations; this law is about things. Everything with software or a connection, from a baby monitor to an industrial controller, must be designed to be secure, must not ship with known holes, and must get security updates. It is the CE safety mark, extended to digital safety.

NL: NIS2 gaat over organisaties; deze wet gaat over dingen. Alles met software of een verbinding, van een babyfoon tot een industriële sturing, moet veilig ontworpen zijn, mag niet met bekende lekken verkocht worden, en moet beveiligingsupdates krijgen. Het is het CE-veiligheidskeurmerk, uitgebreid tot digitale veiligheid.

  • Who: manufacturers, importers and sellers of products with digital parts sold in the EU, wherever they are made.
  • What they must do: secure settings out of the box, no known exploitable weaknesses, security updates for the expected lifetime of the product (in principle at least five years), and a clear end-of-support date.
  • Reporting since 11 September 2026: a manufacturer must report a weakness that is being actively abused within 24 hours, with more detail within 72 hours, through one European platform run by ENISA.
  • Fines: up to €15 million or 2.5% of worldwide turnover.
  • Checks: most products are checked by the maker itself; a list of "important" and "critical" products needs stricter or independent checks.

Where it fell short in 2026: It only covers products sold from 11 December 2027. The freezer controllers, solar inverters and routers already installed stay as they are for years. And for most products the maker still approves itself.

cCybersecurity Act: the agency and the security labels · Cybersecurity Act: het agentschap en de veiligheidslabels

Status: EU regulation 2019/881, in force since 2019. Its successor is being negotiated now (see below).

In plain words: This law did two things. It made ENISA, Europe's cybersecurity agency in Athens, permanent. And it created European security certificates: one test, one label, valid in all 27 countries, so a buyer can see whether a product or service has been checked.

NL: Deze wet deed twee dingen. Ze maakte ENISA, het Europese agentschap voor cyberveiligheid in Athene, permanent. En ze creëerde Europese veiligheidscertificaten: één test, één label, geldig in alle 27 landen, zodat een koper kan zien of een product of dienst gecontroleerd is.

  • ENISA advises, analyses threats, runs exercises such as Cyber Europe, and supports national cyber centres. It does not command them.
  • Certificates are voluntary today. Schemes take years to agree; the one for cloud services has been stuck for years over the question of non-European providers.

Where it fell short in 2026: Voluntary labels did not keep unsafe controllers off the market, and the agency had no task to search for open doors.

dCyber Solidarity Act: help when it goes wrong · Cyber Solidarity Act: hulp als het misgaat

Status: EU regulation 2025/38, in force since 4 February 2025.

In plain words: When a country is overwhelmed by a large attack, it can ask Europe for help. The law sets up a shared alarm system between national monitoring centres, and a reserve of private emergency teams that can be sent to a hospital, an energy company or a ministry.

NL: Als een land overspoeld wordt door een grote aanval, kan het Europa om hulp vragen. De wet richt een gedeeld alarmsysteem op tussen nationale bewakingscentra, en een reserve van private noodteams die naar een ziekenhuis, een energiebedrijf of een ministerie gestuurd kunnen worden.

  • The alert system: national and cross-border "cyber hubs" that share what they see.
  • The EU Cybersecurity Reserve: run by ENISA, with €36 million over three years and teams from 45 European providers; a request must be answered within 48 hours.
  • Review: after a major incident ENISA can be asked to write up what happened and what to learn.

Where it fell short in 2026: €36 million over three years for a whole continent is small: twelve million euros a year. No public record was found of the Reserve being sent to Belgium during the freezer wave.

eThe other European rules that matter · De andere Europese regels die tellen

Status: All in force unless stated.

In plain words: Around those four laws stands a ring of more specific rules: for banks, for the physical protection of vital sites, for electricity, for AI, for online platforms, for product liability, and for punishing foreign attackers.

NL: Rond die vier wetten staat een ring van meer specifieke regels: voor banken, voor de fysieke bescherming van vitale sites, voor elektriciteit, voor AI, voor onlineplatformen, voor productaansprakelijkheid, en voor het bestraffen van buitenlandse aanvallers.

  • DORA (since 17 January 2025): banks, insurers and their key IT suppliers must test their defences and report incidents; European supervisors oversee the biggest IT suppliers directly.
  • Critical Entities Resilience Directive: the physical twin of NIS2: protection of vital sites against sabotage, drones, floods and insiders.
  • Network code on cybersecurity for electricity (2024): a specific rulebook for the organisations that matter for power flows between countries.
  • AI Act: rules for artificial intelligence. Labels on deepfakes apply; the safety rules for high-risk AI were delayed to December 2027 and August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus (in force 27 July 2026).
  • Digital Services Act: large online platforms must assess and reduce risks such as scam adverts, and act on reports.
  • Product Liability Directive: from 9 December 2026 software counts as a product: a maker can be held liable for damage caused by a security flaw or a missing update.
  • Cyber sanctions: the EU can freeze assets and ban travel of those behind attacks. Used on 13 July 2026, together with the UK, against Russia's FSB for the attack on Poland's energy sites.
  • Plans without the force of law: the EU cybersecurity strategy (2020), the crisis "blueprint" for large cross-border incidents (June 2025), and the action plan for the cybersecurity of hospitals (January 2025).

What is being negotiated now

aCybersecurity Act 2 · Cybersecurity Act 2

Status: Proposed by the Commission on 20 January 2026. In Parliament it is with the committee for industry, research and energy (ITRE): the rapporteur, Markéta Gregorová (Greens/EFA, Czechia), presented her draft report on 8 October 2026; amendments closed on 13 October; no committee vote date yet. In the Council the Member States had held 15 working meetings by May 2026 without an agreed position.

In plain words: A rewrite of the 2019 law. It gives ENISA a larger, more practical role, speeds up the security labels, and for the first time lets Europe push suppliers it considers a security risk out of vital networks.

NL: Een herschrijving van de wet van 2019. Ze geeft ENISA een grotere, praktischere rol, versnelt de veiligheidslabels, en laat Europa voor het eerst leveranciers die het als een veiligheidsrisico beschouwt uit vitale netwerken weren.

  • ENISA: from adviser to operator: early warnings, running the Reserve as a permanent task, a European database of weaknesses.
  • Labels: faster schemes. The rapporteur proposes to make certification compulsory by default for certain products.
  • High-risk suppliers: after a risk assessment (started by the Commission or by three or more Member States) a supplier can be listed; telecom operators would get 36 months to remove its key components. In practice aimed at Huawei and ZTE. The rapporteur wants each supplier judged individually, not by country.
  • What Member States dislike: ENISA's wider role, the deadlines, and who decides on high-risk suppliers: the Commission or the governments.
  • What can still be added here: a task for ENISA to search for exposed systems and follow up; compulsory independent testing of devices that connect to the grid; rules for remote access by high-risk suppliers to energy devices.

bNIS2 targeted amendments · Gerichte aanpassingen van NIS2

Status: Proposed on 20 January 2026 together with the Cybersecurity Act 2; same committee and rapporteur. Once adopted, countries get one year to adapt their national laws.

In plain words: A repair job on NIS2, mainly to make it lighter for smaller companies and simpler to report.

NL: Een herstelbeurt voor NIS2, vooral om ze lichter te maken voor kleinere bedrijven en het melden eenvoudiger.

  • A new category of "small mid-cap" companies treated as important instead of essential. The Commission says 28,700 companies would have a lighter load.
  • Extra questions in incident reports about ransomware (was a ransom demanded, was it paid).
  • The rapporteur proposes a single entry point for incident reports.
  • What can still be added here: bringing large food retail into scope; duties by impact instead of company size; a deadline attached to official warnings; two-step login as an explicit minimum.

cPayment Services Regulation · Verordening betalingsdiensten

Status: Political deal in November 2025; Council's first-reading position 28 October 2026; accepted by the Commission on 3 November. Parliament's final vote is next. It will apply roughly 21 months after publication.

In plain words: The rules for banks and payment apps. The new version makes a bank refund a customer when criminals pretend to be that bank, and makes banks check that the name of the receiver matches the account number.

NL: De regels voor banken en betaalapps. De nieuwe versie verplicht een bank om een klant terug te betalen wanneer criminelen zich voordoen als die bank, en om te controleren of de naam van de ontvanger bij het rekeningnummer hoort.

  • Refund when the fraudster impersonated the bank; stronger fraud monitoring; cooperation duties for telecom operators and platforms.
  • It is not a refund for every scam.

dAlso on the table · Ook op tafel

Status: Different stages.

In plain words: Three more files will shape the coming years: who controls government data in the cloud, how much money Europe spends, and whether Europe punishes those behind the freezer sabotage.

NL: Nog drie dossiers bepalen de komende jaren: wie de overheidsgegevens in de cloud controleert, hoeveel geld Europa uitgeeft, en of Europa de verantwoordelijken voor de diepvriessabotage straft.

  • Cloud and AI Development Act (proposed 3 June 2026): four security levels for cloud services used by governments. Early stage; ITRE is involved.
  • The EU budget 2028–2034: Parliament adopted its position on 28 April 2026; a deal between governments is aimed for December 2026. It decides whether there is real money for the Reserve, for hospitals and for testing AI.
  • Sanctions on Iran: France will propose them after its attribution of 9 November 2026. They need all 27 governments.

What Belgium does

aThe Belgian NIS2 law · De Belgische NIS2-wet

Status: Law of 26 April 2024, in force since 18 October 2024. Belgium was among the first to apply NIS2.

In plain words: Belgium's version of NIS2. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) is the national authority: organisations register with it, report to it, and can be inspected by it, together with sector supervisors such as the energy regulator or the nuclear agency.

NL: De Belgische versie van NIS2. Het Centrum voor Cybersecurity België (CCB) is de nationale autoriteit: organisaties registreren zich daar, melden daar, en kunnen door het CCB gecontroleerd worden, samen met sectorale toezichthouders zoals de energieregulator of het nucleair agentschap.

  • About 2,400 organisations had registered by March 2025.
  • 18 April 2026: essential organisations had to hand in a first proof of their security level (a self-assessment under the Belgian CyberFundamentals checklist, or an ISO 27001 file).
  • April 2027: the next step, with verification by an independent body.
  • CyberFundamentals (CyFun): the CCB's free step-by-step checklist, recognised as a way to show compliance.
  • Fines and liability: as in the European text, including personal liability of management.
  • Ethical hackers: since 2023 Belgian law protects people who find a weakness and report it to the CCB under set conditions.

Where it fell short in 2026: Supermarkets and most municipalities are not automatically covered. Three in four hospitals were still below the required level in the January 2026 measurement.

bWho runs it, and what is changing · Wie het leidt, en wat verandert

Status: In motion.

In plain words: The CCB works under the Prime Minister today and moves to the Minister of Security and Home Affairs by 1 January 2027 at the latest. A new national strategy and a new emergency plan set out who does what.

NL: Het CCB werkt vandaag onder de premier en verhuist uiterlijk op 1 januari 2027 naar de minister van Veiligheid en Binnenlandse Zaken. Een nieuwe nationale strategie en een nieuw noodplan leggen vast wie wat doet.

  • National cyber emergency plan: new version adopted by royal decree of 14 April 2026, in force since 7 May 2026, replacing the plan of 2017.
  • National cybersecurity strategy 2026–2030: prepared by the CCB, with the aim of making Belgium one of Europe's least vulnerable countries. In March 2026 it was still waiting for government approval; check whether it has been approved since.
  • Federal Digital Agency: decided on 10 July 2026, with a cybersecurity pillar and a support cell to help public bodies meet NIS2.
  • Critical entities: the Belgian law on the physical protection of vital sites (the twin of NIS2) was reported as adopted in December 2025.
  • Defence: the Cyber Force protects military systems; about €490 million for cyber and encryption in 2026–2034. Belgium is also buying systems against drones for vital sites.

cFor citizens, hospitals and money · Voor burgers, ziekenhuizen en geld

Status: In force or running.

In plain words: Next to the law there are services people can use today, and plans against online fraud.

NL: Naast de wet zijn er diensten die mensen vandaag kunnen gebruiken, en plannen tegen onlinefraude.

  • Safeonweb: citizens forward suspicious messages to verdacht@safeonweb.be; fake sites are then blocked for everyone. More than 40,000 reports a day in 2026.
  • Hospitals: €105 million for hospital security since 2022, and the shared platform SHIELD.
  • Fraud: the banks' action plan (July 2026) and the national plan against online fraud; banks still stop or recover three in four fraudulent phishing transfers.

dFlanders and the municipalities · Vlaanderen en de gemeenten

Status: Regional competence.

In plain words: Local authorities fall under the regions. Flanders pays part of the security audits of its municipalities and has a team that helps a town during an attack.

NL: De lokale besturen vallen onder de gewesten. Vlaanderen betaalt een deel van de veiligheidsaudits van zijn gemeenten en heeft een team dat een gemeente bijstaat tijdens een aanval.

  • Flemish digital security strategy approved on 24 April 2026, covering local authorities.
  • Co-financed audits by Audit Vlaanderen; a Cyber Response Team for local government; the aim that every local authority reaches the "Basic" level of the CCB checklist.

Where it fell short in 2026: More than half of the audited municipalities had no plan to keep working during an attack.

The calendar: what has happened and what is coming

    Cybersecurity Act: ENISA permanent, European security labels.

  2. Dec 2020

    EU cybersecurity strategy.

  3. Jan 2023

    NIS2 enters into force at European level.

  4. 18 Oct 2024

    Belgian NIS2 law applies. Deadline for all countries passed the day before.

  5. 17 Jan 2025

    DORA applies to banks and insurers.

  6. 4 Feb 2025

    Cyber Solidarity Act in force.

  7. Jun 2025

    European crisis blueprint for large cyber incidents.

  8. 20 Jan 2026

  9. 18 Apr 2026

    Belgian essential organisations hand in their first proof of security.

  10. 7 May 2026

    New Belgian cyber emergency plan in force.

  11. 8 Jul 2026

    Commission takes Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to court over NIS2.

  12. 13 Jul 2026

    EU and UK sanction Russia's FSB for the attack on Poland.

  13. 27 Jul 2026

    Digital Omnibus delays the high-risk rules of the AI Act.

  14. 11 Sep 2026

  16. 9 Dec 2026

    Software becomes a "product" under the liability rules.

  17. By 1 Jan 2027

    The CCB moves to the Minister of Security and Home Affairs.

  18. Apr 2027

    Next Belgian NIS2 step: independent verification.

  19. 11 Dec 2027

    Every new connected product must be secure by law.

  20. Dec 2027 / Aug 2028

    High-risk rules of the AI Act apply.

  21. 2028

    New EU budget period starts.

Where the system still falls short

  • Organisations outside the rules: supermarket retail, most municipalities, and small firms that control many devices for others.
  • Devices outside the rules: everything installed before December 2027.
  • Warnings without force: the cyber centre can warn, but outside NIS2 it cannot order anyone to act or set a deadline.
  • Uneven application: four large countries had not turned NIS2 into national law by July 2026.
  • A small emergency team: €36 million over three years for the whole EU.
  • Slow labels: security certificates are voluntary and take years.
  • AI: the safety rules for high-risk AI were pushed back to the end of 2027 and 2028.

Each gap is worked out on the page "What we lack", with the ideas that would close it.

Names and numbers to keep straight

  • NIS2 = organisations. Cyber Resilience Act = products. Cybersecurity Act = the agency ENISA and the labels. Cyber Solidarity Act = emergency help.
  • 24 hours: the time a vital organisation has to give a first warning of a serious attack.
  • €10 million or 2%: the top fine under NIS2. €15 million or 2.5%: under the Cyber Resilience Act.
  • 11 December 2027: safe devices compulsory.
  • 20 January 2026: the date of the proposal now in Parliament's industry committee (ITRE).
  • ENISA is in Athens and advises; it does not command the national cyber centres.

ransomwareCriminal software that locks your files and demands money to unlock them.Gijzelsoftware: criminele software die je bestanden vergrendelt en geld eist om ze vrij te geven.

In plain words · In gewone woorden

The EU laws being negotiated right now, where each one stands in the process, and what could still be added to it.

NL: De EU-wetten waarover nu onderhandeld wordt, hoe ver elk dossier staat, en wat er nog aan toegevoegd kan worden.
